subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 266, to provide for the operation and maintenance of a residence for the Prime Minister of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill provides for the maintenance and operation of the prime minister's residence. When the resolution was being considered yesterday there was some discussion about the construction of the house. I would point out that such discussion is not pertinent to this bill. Parliament has decided to construct a residence for the prime minister, and the house was informed that it was the intention to remodel an existing residence for that purpose. The problem that faced the government in connection with this property was similar on a smaller scale to that which faced the government of the United States with regard to the remodelling of the White House. It was known that it would be much cheaper to tear down the White House and rebuild it, but it was decided that in view of the historic aspect of the White House, the government would proceed to spend $4 million in remodelling the present structure rather than building a new house for about half of that sum.
I am not suggesting that the two cases are entirely parallel; however, there was
8, 1950	3343
Official Residence for Prime Minister some reluctance about tearing down one of Ottawa's fine older houses and replacing it with a new building. Consequently the cost of remodelling the house is whatever the cost must be. The government has appointed a reliable firm of architects with wide experience in building better-class houses, and has appointed a responsible firm of local contractors to do the building. The work is being supervised by the architects, as well as by a clerk of the Department of Public Works. I believe, therefore, a discussion of the cost of building this residence is not pertinent to this bill.
The question does arise, however, of the position of the prime minister in living in that residence. We have looked up precedents and we find that in England the prime minister is provided with two houses, one at 10 Downing street and the other at Chequers, both of which are wholly maintained by the government. In England the practice goes even further, in that a number of flats throughout London are provided for cabinet ministers and maintained at public expense. I am not suggesting any extension of the prime minister's residence principle in Ottawa; I simply draw that to the attention of the house as a precedent for the position we are now considering.
In the United States the White House is maintained by the government and a skeleton staff is provided by the government. The president .pays for the remainder of the staff and provides for the running expenses of the house. I point out that for that purpose he can draw on an expense account of $75,000 per annum, which is placed at his disposal to be used at his discretion.
The Prime Minister of Canada has no personal expense account.	The Prime
Minister does not wish to be better off as a result of occupying this residence than he is today, and has therefore insisted that he make a payment for the use of the house. According to the provisions contained in the bill the house will be maintained by the Department of Public Works, as to heating and repairs; the grounds will be maintained and improved from time to time by the federal district commission.	The government will appoint a steward for the house, who will engage the necessary staff and provide the services that are required in the house.
No doubt a question will be asked as to why the prime minister's annual payment is fixed at $5,000. Several considerations were taken into account. One was that the salary of the prime minister is fixed at $15,000 per year, whereas the salary of a cabinet minister is fixed at $10,000 per year. It was felt
3344	HOUSE OF
Official Residence for Prime Minister that the $5,000 would cover the additional expenses the prime minister would have above those of other cabinet ministers, and that that sum might be a fair gauge of the amount that the prime minister should contribute in return for having a house and living provided in Ottawa. There was also the fact that a man living in Ottawa, who finds it necessary to maintain a home elsewhere, would spend about that amount for living accommodation in the capital.
The bill provides that the prime minister will pay a rental covering food and lodging for the prime minister's residence of $5,000 per annum. I believe that what I have said explains the objects of this bill. Members in all parts of the house were desirous that the prime minister should have a home in Ottawa, which would belong to the government, and which would be a type of house befitting his position. It is ridiculous to ask a man living on a cabinet minister's salary- which I may say has not been increased in the last thirty years, and incidentally I am not complaining about that fact-to maintain at his private expense the type of house that is being provided for the prime minister.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was unfortunately absent when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) began to speak. I understand that he suggested that it was not seemly to be inquisitive about the cost of the prime minister's residence. Let me say what I said yesterday, that I think everyone in this house wants the prime minister to have a dignified residence. I agree fully with what the minister has said about the prime minister being treated in a most generous manner. I would not cavil about the allowance which he is paying. As a matter of fact, I would not have cavilled if he were not paying anything. That is one aspect of this matter. But when it comes to the other aspect of it, which is an expenditure apparently well into $500,000, then to suggest, if the minister did suggest it, that we are really doing this, as the boys say, "sight unseen", I do not think is reasonable. So far it seems to me we have had no intelligible picture of this transaction. Yesterday everyone on the opposite side of the house who had anything to do with it seemed to pass the ball to somebody else.
I just want to say that when we get into committee we should have the details of this transaction put before us in a reasonable and intelligible manner. Up to the present time I think the only piece of definite information we have is that the coach house, or whatever it is, in front of the residence, is not to be used for the residence of a secretary. That may be highly interesting, but it does not


really cover the whole case. I therefore wish to say that I think we are entitled to an intelligible and detailed statement of the cost.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: When this matter was before the house, Mr. Speaker, on September 30 last, all parties in the house were in agreement that the Prime Minister of Canada should be provided with a suitable residence at public expense. The site that was chosen is, in my opinion, one of the most beautiful in the city of Ottawa, and is in every way suitable for such a residence. On September 30 I said, as reported at page 385 of Hansard, that I thought the government would be well advised to build a new house, with modern conveniences, and perhaps more suitable for the purpose in mind, instead of reconditioning or rebuilding the interior of an old house. I knew this particular piece of property when I spoke about it on that occasion. Yesterday at noon, after the discussion in the house, I went to see the property again and took a look at it. I think that a mistake was made in not demolishing the old house, and building something more in keeping with the purse-strings of future prime ministers of this country and perhaps of even the present Prime Minister of Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: You are one hundred per cent right on that.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I think the government itself may be disappointed at the cost of reconditioning this building, in spite of what was said to me yesterday as a matter of fact by one of the officials to the effect that this might be considered to be an historic building. It is of course different from the White House in the United States in that respect, because it has no history of any sort behind it which would recommend it to the public of Canada.
I also want to agree with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) when he said that we should scrutinize the terms of this bill. It seems to me that it would be far better had we had a more modest arrangement and not included in the bill the $5,000 provision. I think that looks rather small on the part of this parliament. I can understand why the government put this provision in the bill, although I think it would have been better to leave the matter entirely open so that it could be dealt with, if it was felt necessary to do so, in some other way.
I want to say this, however. The emoluments of the Prime Minister of Canada, in comparison with those of some other offices under the crown, are exceedingly modest. We have for example, the governor of the Bank of Canada. I do not know exactly what his emoluments are, but I believe that they are

at least twice as much as the salary the Prime Minister of Canada receives. Then we have the emoluments of the president of the Canadian National Railways, and they are, I believe, three times as much as the Prime Minister of Canada receives. Consequently I feel rather badly about this $5,000 provision.
I am all in favour of our providing a suitable residence but, as I said before, I think a bad mistake has been made. We may criticize the expenditure and the cost of this building as much as we will, but the deed is done. The building is there. It is being remodelled, and I must say from what I saw yesterday that the minister was quite right when he said we have a competent firm of architects who are doing the best they can with an old building which, when they looked into it, was found to be in relatively poor condition. Much more had to be done in the strengthening of the walls and all the rest of it than was expected. The government made a bad guess, and whatever we can do now will not rectify the results of that guess. I am therefore suggesting that we must accept the situation as we find it and give consideration to the provisions of the bill.
I think our country is doing the proper thing, in conformity with what other countries have done, in providing the first citizen of this country with a residence in which he may receive distinguished guests from at home and abroad.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
should like to say a word about this matter, Mr. Speaker, in the first place because I intend to move an amendment to the bill when it comes before us. I believe I am in order in saying that I am going to move an amendment.
I come from a rural riding where we do not have pretentious places, but I object strenuously to that $5,000 provision, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I intend to move an amendment that the rental be $1 a year. After all, it does not matter what party is in power; the leader of that party is the Prime Minister of Canada, in a position analogous to that of the president of the United States. Naturally I hope that none of the parties opposite will be in power. But if they are, the people in my riding, and I as an individual member, will pay respect to the position held by the leader of it, whatever party it may be.
As the leader of the C.C.F. stated when he spoke last year, if I remember correctly, it would have been better to tear the old building down and build a new one. Two wrongs, however, do not make a right. We have

Official Residence for Prime Minister a skeleton out there now, and the best we can do is to make it a credit to Canada, in keeping with the position we hold in the United Nations.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, I intend to move in amendment that the rental be $1, not $5,000, for the Prime Minister of Canada, whoever he may be and to whatever party he may belong.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the house has to distinguish between two things in approaching the second reading of this bill. On the simple issue whether the country should provide an official residence for the prime minister, I am quite certain that there will be no disagreement or difference of opinion in this house. If that were the sole principle of this bill, then of course it would be entitled to command unanimous support on second reading. But, sir, this bill goes further than that. This bill proposes to make a particular property in Ottawa the official residence. The bill sets out in detail a description of the property by metes and bounds. Therefore it seems to me that the acting leader of the government is quite wrong in saying, as he has intimated . this morning, that the house should not concern itself with an examination of this particular property as to the cost, and the expenditures made upon it, in trying to fit it for use as the official residence for the prime minister.
There is one particular correction that I should like to make in the remarks of the right hon. gentleman. Early in, his remarks this morning he used these words: "The house has decided to construct a residence." That may have been simply a slip of the tongue. What the house has intimated, informally to date it is true, is that it approves the idea of providing a residence. It seems to me that there was no suggestion in anything that has been said so far in the house that the selection of this particular property was approved; nor was the method that the government has pursued in renovating the property, and spending vast sums of money thereon, approved.
The acting leader of the government did not buttress his case one little bit this morning, sir, by bringing in the argument about historical values, and setting up the White House at Washington as an example. Certainly the White House at Washington is of the greatest historical interest. That would be a factor of leading importance to the government of the United States in deciding whether that building should be renovated or replaced by an entirely new building. Is anyone going to say that this particular property, the former Edwards residence, has such

Official Residence for Prime Minister historical value to the whole people of Canada that it must be maintained in its present form? I think that argument does not add one little bit to the strength of the case put forward by the acting leader of the government.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well) has said:	"True, the government
has made a bad guess; but here we are faced with an accomplished fact, and we have to accept it." Sir, it goes a good deal beyond a very bad guess on the part of the government. The government has botched this whole undertaking from the beginning. The idea started off on a perfectly sound basis, and then was mishandled to the point where it is very difficult, in a bill of this kind, for some hon. members to give approval to it when they realize that by giving approval to it they have to overlook completely the botch that the government has made of it.
I think it is time, sir, to face this situation very clearly. What the government has done is this: Without asking for specific approval of parliament, without bringing before the house last fall, as it should have done, a bill to set aside a particular property, if they thought that was the best property, they made an announcement in the house without mentioning anything of that idea. They proceeded by order in council to set aside a house that had been acquired by the government several years before by expropriation for a purpose that we did not then know, and then proceeded with the work of renovation. All that was said in the house on that occasion, on September 30, by anybody who spoke in the house was that the idea that the government should provide at the expense of the country an official residence for the Prime Minister was approved; but no one went beyond that. Whatever has been done in regard to selecting this property, whatever has been done in the way of expenditure of vast sums of money upon it to try to modernize an ancient house, has been done solely on the responsibility of the government and without any approval on the part of this house.
Now, sir, what exactly has the government done? The right hon. gentleman said this morning that the cost is not pertinent. Sir, that is an extraordinary proposition, when we are asked as a House of Commons to-

speechtext: I have not changed one iota of the sentence of the right hon. gentleman. What he said, sir, in a very plain statement to the house this morning was that the cost was not pertinent to the discussion of this bill this morning. There is no member in the house who could draw any other inference from it.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: You did.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I submit that no hon. member can dismiss from his mind questions in regard to costs or the method of dealing with this property, in addressing himself to his responsibility in relation to this bill.
What did the government do, entirely on its own responsibility? I have said in the first place that by order in council they set aside a government-owned property for this purpose. I remember the occasion in the life of the last parliament when the exchequer court established the amount to be paid by the government on expropriation of this property. I believe the figure was $140,000. Being of an inquisitive turn of mind I remember rising and asking the prime minister at that time for what purpose the government intended to use the property. The answer was completely evasive. Nobody knew by the time the then prime minister had finished what the property was to be used for.
The government has taken the responsibility by saying this is to be the property which will be used as a residence for the prime minister. So far as the physical situation of the land is concerned, everyone I am sure will agree with what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said this morning, that it is a beautiful property, is handsomely located and from that point of view is very suitable. But what about the house? Would it not have been common sense on the part of anybody who has any claim to using his sense in reference to business to sit down first and -try to count the cost? That is one thing this government did not do. They make no pretence of having done it. What they did was to decide, again without any consultation with or approval by parliament, that they would maintain the existing structure. So far as we are told, they did not ask for the preparation of any plans or for the submission of estimates on the cost of construction of a suitable modern residence. Apparently that did not enter into the scope of consideration on the part of the government. They just decided they were going to take this old building-I am told

it is eighty years old. It goes back almost to the time of confederation. Perhaps that is what the acting leader of the government meant this morning when he talked about historical interest, an eighty-year old building-and they started in to disembowel it and tried to make an ancient structure suitable for use as a modern residence.
What is the cost? Well, at least at that stage one would have thought they would seek to have some estimate of the cost. Having failed to exercise any elementary sense of business in not ascertaining the cost of constructing a modern counterpart of such an ancient edifice, the number two mistake, the number two blunder was this. They did not even have an estimate of the cost of this type of renovation and reconstruction, because it is a major job of reconstruction, let there be no mistake about that. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) told this house that the alterations and improvements to the main building, so he was told, will cost $135,000. He also told the house that that was only an estimate. But, sir, let the house be quite clear on this. It was not an estimate given before the work was undertaken. The government decided on this task of renovation and reconstruction without having a firm estimate before them of the cost of construction. The government do not know even today what it is going to cost. They cannot even tell us exactly what the renovation of the grounds is going to cost. They cannot tell us today what the furnishings in the residence are going to cost; they cannot tell us in fact anything that I think most hon. members of this house making any claim to business sense would want to know or would have asked at the very outset of this undertaking before they gave approval to it. So I say that this government has taken a sound idea, an idea which will command general acceptance, the idea that the country ought to provide a suitable residence for the Prime Minister of Canada, and from that point on has proceeded to botch the whole job.
It may be that we are now faced with a situation from which it is difficult to retreat. I feel that there is only one way for me to vote on section 5. Until the emoluments of the office of prime minister of this country are increased from $15,000 to $25,000 or $30,000 per year, I shall have to vote against the section. I believe that this country is not being fair to the prime minister. As an example, I could cite men in my constituency who are working for large corporations and Who are receiving from two to three times the salary of the prime minister of this country. I believe those people deserve all they are getting, they are worthy of their hire, for they are working for large mining and corporation interests. I repeat that I do not see how it is possible for this committee to pass section 5 without a promise that parliament will rectify the anomaly that I have just mentioned.
During the general discussion on the first section of the bill, some members mentioned the cost of the food. Surely Canada ought to be able to provide adequately for the prime minister without quibbling about such details as the cost of the food. After all, we voted tremendous sums of money to send food to other countries for which we do not expect any repayment and over which expenditure we practically have no control. Surely it is the duty of this parliament to see to it that if this item is passed, then within a reasonable time, and not later than early next session, the emoluments of the office of prime minister and of the members of the cabinet are properly dealt with.
Someone said that a future prime minister might not be able to pay $5,000 a year. We parliamentarians realize what it means to be mere members of parliament and the calls that are made upon us. I may say that I am satisfied with what I am receiving


as a member of parliament, but how much money can any member save if he accedes to the requests made of him, and logically made, by his constituents?
On the other hand, consider the position of the prime minister, who always keeps himself at the entire disposal of every citizen and organization of this country. Let us visualize for a moment what the establishment of this government house will mean. It will come next to Rideau Hall as the rendezvous of officials, the place for receptions for prominent people from Canada and the rest of the world. Surely, we cannot afford to be niggardly about a matter of this kind.
Mention was made during the discussion of the estimated cost of the house, $100,000 or $200,000. If we cannot afford to provide proper accommodation for our prime minister, and to see that he gets a salary befitting his office, then this parliament does not seem to be fulfilling its duty in relation to matters such as this. The only way I can vote for section 5 is to have a promise that the emoluments of the office of prime minister will be increased before the next session. I am sure the majority of the people would wish that this be done.

speechtext:
When the estimates of the Department of National Defence were up for consideration on March 17, I did not have an opportunity of making any general remarks, and I propose to take the opportunity of making them now.
During past sessions members of this party have made several suggestions for improvement, as we saw it, of the defence forces of the country. I am glad to see that some of these suggestions have been or are being followed to some extent. Last year in particular the hon. member for Nanaimo urged that much greater attention should be paid to the development of the air arm. He urged that a larger proportion of the defence dollar should be spent on that service, and that equipment in considerably increased amount should be provided for it. During these past several months I have noticed that the minister has spoken about this matter on numerous occasions, and has made quite a point of the fact that there has been a considerable increase in the amount of the defence dollar devoted to the air force. Apparently he has been anxious to assure everyone in the country that the air force is getting what we might call major attention amongst the three services.

On several occasions in the past I have criticized the top-heavy organization of the Department of National Defence. By this I meant particularly the fact that in my opinion an unduly large number of officers and men were employed at the various headquarters and in administrative duties, with the result that relatively few people were in the fighting units. The minister has indicated that some changes in that regard are in progress or are contemplated. It was, of course, one of the recommendations of the Mainguy report that, with regard to the navy, a considerable number of naval officers employed at headquarters should be relieved from what we might call desk duties so that they could devote their time to active sea duties.
When the minister comes to answer questions in detail or reply to the various speeches that were made last March 17, I hope he will tell us more specifically what progress has been made in that direction and what is the ratio, as we might call it, between the number of persons in the actual fighting units and the number of persons on administrative and other duties at headquarters and so forth, particularly breaking the figures down to show what has been done in each of the three services. I think there is just as much necessity for that procedure in the army as there is for it in the navy, if not more. I must say that I do not know very much about the situation as to the air force, but I suspect it is much the same.
On November 11,	1949, the minister
enunciated the defence policy of Canada. It may be found in Hansard of that date at page 1663. I should like to make some comments on that defence policy and ask some questions in connection with it. In order to have continuity perhaps I had better read the seven points which the minister enunciated at that time. They are as follows:
1.	The only possible aggressor is the Soviet union.
2.	Any war would be a world war involving all western peoples who would be fighting for their survival as nations and their freedom as men.
3.	The best way to prevent such war is to confront the forces of communism with such strength as to deter them from attack.
4.	To provide such strength requires the cooperative efforts of the western nations, including the United States and Canada.
5.	Consequently Canada welcomed the North Atlantic treaty as supplementing the United Nations, and pending the strengthening of the United Nations, as an organization for world-wide security.
These five points are what you might call general points. They deal with basic concepts of what we look upon as facts. Later I shall have something to say in connection with them in relation to what our present concepts are, whether there has been any change in them or not, and so on.
Supply-National Defence
The sixth and seventh points are really the operative ones, the ones which concern the defence forces and what to quite an extent we are discussing.
The sixth one is:
6.	Since an attack on Canada could only be made by air or by sea, emphasis must be placed on defence forces: by air-radar stations and communications, backed by interceptors and a relatively small mobile brigade group; by sea-anti-submarine and anti-mine vessels for protection of shipping and coastal waters.
The seventh is:
7.	The best place to defeat the enemy is as far away from Canada as possible, and our forces should also serve as the nucleus for the development of our maximum potential.
In connection with the sixth point, which concerns particularly the permanent force, I should like the minister at a later time to indicate whether we have the radar stations and communications, the interceptors and the small mobile brigade group which are necessary to guard again any likely attack on Canada. In my opinion we have not. When the minister is replying I should like him to say, if we have not what is required at the moment, how much progress we have made toward getting it, and what we actually have. I think the committee is entitled to know just what we have in that regard. The same thing applies so far as the remainder of that point is concerned, namely, "by sea-antisubmarine and anti-mine vessels for protection of shipping and coastal waters". We should know definitely what vessels of that kind we have, and what they are capable of doing.
In introducing his estimates on March 17 the minister said that we have two interceptor squadrons at the present time and five more in mind, so that we would have seven all told. I should like to know whether the two squadrons we have at the present time are up to strength, both in men and in planes, or are they at quarter strength or half strength? As to the other five which are proposed, what progress has been made on them? Are they merely on paper, or have the nucleus staffs for them been got together? Have any planes been secured for them?
To revert to these more general aims of our defence policy, I asked last year, when we were considering defence matters, what our commitments were under the Atlantic pact. The minister replied at that time that we had none. It was interesting to note that about the same time that the defence discussion was going on in the house, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was down in New York where he made a speech at the United Nations, I think, in which he made reference to the commitments involved in the Atlantic
3356	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence pact, United Nations membership, and so forth. The result was this. I heard that somebody, having read in the press that the Minister of National Defence had said that we had no commitments for defence under the Atlantic pact, asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs this question: "Well, when is a commitment not a commitment?" That is still an appropriate query. When is a commitment not a commitment? We seem to be in a considerable amount of confusion as to what commitments we have under the United Nations, the North Atlantic treaty, and so forth. It is a matter which needs some clarification.
In his speech on November 17 the minister reiterated the statement that we had no commitments. I should like to read what he said at that time, as found at page 851 of Hansard, and to comment on it. He said:
Under the North Atlantic treaty we have not made any specific commitment, but we have given the general undertaking contained in article 3 of the treaty to take such action as we deem necessary by means of continuous and effective self-help and mutual aid to maintain and develop individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack. A second undertaking, as contained in article 5, comes into effect in the event of an armed attack against one or more of the signatories. That undertaking is to take such action as we deem necessary to restore and maintain the security of the north Atlantic area.
I take it that that means briefly just two things. First, we have undertaken self-help. That means the defence of Canada. We are going to look after our own borders. Second, it means that we have undertaken to take such action as we ourselves believe to be necessary for the common defence of the north Atlantic countries in the event of an attack upon any one of them. Only under these circumstances do we agree to pay any attention to what we might call mutual defence, other than protecting our own borders. It seems to me that this concept, and our entire defence planning, must be materially altered by the decisions which were taken in London last month, as set forth in the speech made in the house on Monday last by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
In connection with what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said about defence particularly, there are these three short sentences that I should like to read; they are to be found at page 3189 of Hansard:
We have adopted the principle of "balanced collective forces1' as the basis for our defence.


That is for all the north Atlantic countries, and he was speaking in the house particularly so far as Canada is concerned. Further on he said:
We shall try to agree amongst ourselves which of us is the best able to concentrate on certain types of defence preparation.
I take it from that that each of the countries in the North Atlantic pact is going to concentrate on certain types of defence-to specialize on them, one might say. I take it also that Canada must follow that line and specialize in some certain line of defence, or at least direct the major portion of our defence effort to a certain line or certain lines of defence.
Then, a little further on-and perhaps this is the most important observation he made- the minister said this:
North Atlantic strategy cannot mean, and our agreement does not imply a strategy of liberation after destruction and occupation. There could be no hope for Europe in that strategy, because the next time there may well be nothing to liberate.
That means that the strategy agreed upon would be such as to prevent the overrunning of western European countries by the forces of Russia. It is of course obvious that in order to do that, the countries of the North Atlantic pact must have forces which can go in and stop any Russian advance over those countries. If we in Canada have any definite commitment to put that strategy into effect-and from the speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs I take it we have -this means that we must have forces which could be thrown into the struggle immediately.
We have abandoned the concept, which the Minister of National Defence has expressed before, that we have a small permanent force capable of meeting any diversionary raids which may be directed at our country, and looking after What might be called limited local defence; and, in addition, we were to have a framework upon which we could build up comparatively large forces which we could then send overseas in the general defence of western Europe.
If the new concept in strategy placed before us on Monday means anything at all, it must mean that in future we must have forces which can be dispatched at once. It would seem to me that the only forces which we could throw into action immediately would be air forces. Therefore, to a much greater extent than we have done up to the moment we would have to concentrate upon the development of our air arm. In addition I should think it would mean that if we are going to make to general western defence

a contribution commensurate with our ability, we would have to have a considerably larger number of air squadrons. Otherwise we could not make this initial effort which would be required.
Further, it would mean that the only other type of force which could be thrown into action immediately and effectively would be specialized armoured forces, so far as land forces are concerned, and especially airborne forces.
I suggest that the minister should make some comment on what this new strategy of defending western Europe from invasion, rather than liberating it afterward, would involve in our defence planning. What changes in our defence program are going to flow from this change in strategy? If we are to have a great deal more equipment capable of being thrown in immediately when required, it would cost us a great deal more money. This year 'we are being asked to vote very large sums for defence; but if the new strategy is to be followed effectively by us, then we shall probably be required to provide much larger sums to implement our part of the program.
There is one further point I should like to make in this connection. One of the most important considerations in the strategy set out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the protection of western Europe is what is to be done with western Germany. Russia is now arming the Germans in the Russian zone of Germany. In my opinion the decision is squarely up to the Atlantic pact nations to do the same thing in the western zone or, if we are not prepared at the present time to arm the Germans in our zone, we must accept the proposition that none of the western zone of Germany can be defended. We shall have to write it off in the beginning as an area to be overrun by the Russians, in the event of war with them.
Personally I think it is also extremely unlikely that, without the armed manpower of western Germany, any of the western European nations with the exception of the peninsulas-Italy, possibly, and more likely Spain, and of course Great Britain because of her island position-could be held successfully. But apart from those countries it would seem to me most unlikely that the North Atlantic pact countries, as the strategy enunciated suggests, could be saved from occupation unless that large pool of manpower in western Germany is utilized.
I should like to know whether this aspect of the matter has been considered in formulating our defence policy, and whaf the conclusions have been with respect thereto. I know that this whole question is a very thorny one,
Supply-National Defence concerning which most governments in western Europe do not wish to commit themselves, because there is still a large body of opinion mortally afraid of a rearmed Germany. However, in my view this is one of the most important questions to be faced-indeed, perhaps the vital one-if this new strategy is to be carried into effect.
If our government has any opinion in the matter, then we should be told about it in the House of Commons. If our military leaders have anything like the view I have enunciated, we should be told. If they do take that view, then we as a country should be prepared to press for its adoption. Someone has to take the lead in these matters, and, well removed from Europe, without any undue internal difficulty, we could quite readily take that lead, whereas, in a country like France the internal difficulty would be much greater.
This year the estimates were introduced early-and it was a good move. I had hoped that when on March 17 we began a discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Defence, such discussion would be continued shortly thereafter so that the entire estimates of the department might be dealt with more or less as a whole instead of having them broken up. But we find that this year the same thing is happening that has happened every other year I have been here. Almost three months has elapsed since the defence estimates were last discussed. We are now proceeding to consider them under circumstances which the minister described as terminal pressure. He tried to refute the statement made, I believe, by an hon. member in this party, that the defence estimates have always been considered right at the end of the session when there has been no time to deal with them properly. He made a lengthy statement which is to be found at page 755 of Hansard of March 14. At that time he indicated on what dates the estimates had been dealt with. I looked up those dates and compared them with the closing dates of the sessions, and I found that in each case these estimates had been considered a short time before the end of the session, and at a time when we were sitting, as we are now, in morning, afternoon and evening, with the committees sitting as well. I hope the minister will not try to argue that we are not under terminal pressure at the present time; we are under considerable terminal pressure. The suggestion this year that the estimates, particularly those of this department, which was the first one to be introduced, would be dealt with before the terminal pressure came on, when we could take the time required to deal with them without difficulty, has not

Supply-National Defence been carried out. We are faced with the same situation as that with which we have been faced every other year.
This year the expenditures under this department are lumped in two large items which are the only items that really amount to anything. The first item covers all expenditures for the army, navy and air force, while the second item covers defence research and development. I referred to this matter last year, and asked the minister to consider introducing his estimates in the same manner as those of other departments, and in the same manner as they were presented before the war and even during the war. This should be possible now that the war has been over for some time and the rehabilitation and reorganization period is almost completed. These expenditures should be broken down into separate items instead of being lumped together.
This method of indicating the expenditures does not present as good a picture to hon. members as would be presented if the estimates were shown in the ordinary way. It does not show how many people are employed in the different branches, what their jobs are, and so forth. There is a certain breakdown in the back of the book, but it does not give any of this information. As a result it is much more difficult for members to know just how the money is being spent by the Department of National Defence, and it becomes necessary to ask many more questions and take up more time than would otherwise be taken.
Last year the minister said that serious consideration would be given to breaking up the estimates for the coming year, but nothing has been done. I ask once more that this be done in the future. I see no reason why it should not be done in this department as it is done in the other departments. Unfortunately there has been a tendency throughout to give as little information as possible in regard to this department. The minister has maintained consistently that that is not so, but everything points to the fact that it is.
I should like to say a word about recruiting. When the minister was speaking in the debate on the proposal to set up a committee on national defence he said, as reported on page 758 of Hansard of March 14:
I believe it was the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) who said that if a committee were established it would help recruiting. Our recruiting for the active forces, the navy, army and air force, does not need any help. We are getting all the men we want. They are first-class men of fine character.
I was surprised to hear the minister make that statement. I should have thought he would have been glad to get all the help he

could. I was particularly surprised at the statement because at that time, and I think this still applies, the minister was carrying on an extensive advertising campaign for recruits. There was also a radio program, about which the hon. member for Temiscouata made quite a lengthy speech. I heard it myself at various times. Large advertisements were carried in the newspapers, and so on. All this must have been very costly, and when we are dealing with the details later I shall want to know what this campaign cost.
In view of the fact that this advertising campaign was going on at the time, it was surprising that the minister should say he did not want or need any help in the matter of recruiting, that they were getting all the men they wanted. If that was so, why were they putting on this extensive advertising campaign? I do know that a large number of the reserve force units require men, and in that connection I think the minister should welcome any help.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the committee adjourned at one o'clock I was dealing with certain points covered in the speech the minister made on March 14. Before going on with that I should like to revert for a moment to a matter I dealt with earlier.
Speaking of the strategic concept adopted by the Atlantic pact nations at London last month to prevent the occupation of western Europe by Russian forces in the event of war, I overlooked one point which I should like to mention now. While the utilization of German manpower and fighting capabilities is, I think, the crux of carrying out such a policy and making it effective, the absence of Spain from the western military bloc is a serious defect. Up to the present time ideological differences between that country and the democratic countries of western Europe and North America have prevented the military co-operation that is desirable. I do not think ideological differences should

any longer prevent us from securing the advantages which close co-operation with Spain in western defence would bring about.
During the war we were very glad of Russian aid when fighting for our survival against Germany. The question of ideological differences between us and the communist countries did not enter into the picture at that time. With the situation we now face of extreme danger from Russian imperialistic ambitions I think the same attitude should be adopted and that steps should be taken to make Spain and its resources available to the western powers. If it were impossible to carry out the strategic concept of preventing the occupation of the other countries of western Europe, possibly the one country which could be defended and kept as a bridgehead in Europe is Spain. In the over-all strategy of planning for defence it seems to me a most important matter that steps should be taken at the present time to put Spain in a position to contribute materially toward that end. For example, there should be large airfields constructed in Spain from which our air fleets could operate, and also strategic roads leading to the border. This matter should receive careful attention from the Atlantic powers generally and our own defence administration. They might put forward that point of view, if it is agreeable to them.
With reference to the minister's speech of March 17, he mentioned that standardization of battle procedures and organization was going forward. When he speaks later I should like him to tell us exactly on what basis that is taking place. Is standardization general throughout the Atlantic pact countries, or is it a matter on our part of standardization with the United States forces, and the adoption by us of their battle procedures in lieu of the British battle procedures which so far we have used? The minister said at the same time that standardization of equipment was necessarily slow, and I can see that would be so. I should think the amounts of military equipment now being shipped and about to be shipped from the United States to European countries would speed up that process to a considerable extent.
The minister made note of an offer on the part of Canada to train officers from other countries on somewhat the same basis as the empire air training scheme. Provision is to be made for the training of 150 ground officers and 100 air officers of other countries. I think that is a good move in the direction of standardization, but actually it is a very small one. When he is dealing with this point it would perhaps be of interest if the minister could tell us how many
Supply-National Defence Canadian officers are receiving training in other countries at the present time, and what their services are.
The minister also made a statement in connection with the successful development of a Canadian jet plane, the CF-100. I am sure his announcement was received with great satisfaction by everyone in the house and elsewhere in Canada. Personally I am very happy that we are now producing a really up-to-date jet military plane. I trust that production will be sufficiently great that we shall be able to put large numbers of these machines into service in the near future.
The minister gave an interesting account of Exercise Sweetbriar. I am sure the committee was pleased to hear his report. He said that in our northern areas defence forces have the advantage, but in order to make that advantage effective they must be able .to prevent the leapfrogging of the enemy from one airfield to another. That suggests to me this question. Have we the air force, the airborne infantry and other arms to prevent such leapfrogging? In other words, is our mobile brigade group of sufficient strength to do it at the present time, and even if it were at full strength, would it be sufficient to carry out that task?
In dealing with Exercise Sweetbriar the minister also spoke of the need for more tracked vehicles. He mentioned bulldozers particularly, and indicated that probably at least one per company would be necessary. I should like to ask what has been done since that time to provide not only bulldozers but also other tracked vehicles capable of travelling over snow.
The minister said that the target for our forces is to become more and more operational. Of course that is something which we on this side of the house have urged ever since the post-war army was established. I think there will be many questions as. to the extent to which it has been accomplished. As I mentioned previously, a reduction in the number of officers and men in headquarters administration establishment and an increase in the number in the fighting units would be an important step in that direction.
With regard to the amount of the defence dollar which is being divided among the three services, there appears to be a discrepancy in the figures given by the minister. He said that in the past year, 1949-50, the air force was receiving 42-6 per cent of the defence dollar, while in the current year, 1950-51, they will receive 44-8 per cent. This statement appears on page 858 of Hansard of March 17, 1950. On page 857 of Hansard there is a chart which shows the distribution
3360	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence of the defence dollar. For the year 1949-50 it shows the air force receiving 38'8 per cent rather than the 42-6 per cent the minister mentioned, and for 1950-51 it shows the air force receiving 40-6 per cent rather than the 44-8 per cent. I should like the minister to explain that apparent discrepancy.
During the course of his statement the minister said that over one-half of the army 'brigade group were now tough, trained soldiers. That statement does not mean very much unless we know three other things. Is this half the present strength of the brigade group, or is it half the authorized strength? If the latter, is the authorized strength at the present time the full strength for the brigade group? Until we know those things, this general statement that over half the brigade group are tough, trained soldiers does not mean very much. If it were the first -case I mentioned there would be a smaller number involved than if it were the last. I should like some further light on that point.
There was a statement that defence research was carried on on an increased scale during the past year. No details were given to indicate on what line defence research was conducted, what increase there may have been, or anything else. I think the committee is entitled to a full explanation. We all agree that defence research is one of the most important bases of national defence at the present time. So far as I have been able to observe in the house, it is a phase which there has been no disposition to cut down at all. The disposition has been the other way, to increase it.
The minister also made a brief statement about civilian defence planning. He said that it had progressed satisfactorily and had finished at the federal level, I think it was, or something to that effect.
At page 859 of Hansard of March 17, 1950, the minister stated:
In civil defence we have completed the stage of planning at the federal level. Civil defence depends on close co-operation with the provinces, the municipalities and other agencies at every level. Following earlier preliminary discussions we are now in a position to make further progress.
I believe the minister will recall that I have spoken on this subject at length in each of the past three or four sessions. I believe that civilian defence is, in some ways, more important than any other phase of defence activities or defence planning. The statement that in civil defence we have completed the stage of planning at the federal level does not convey a great deal, and I should like to know what it implies. I know that General Worthington has been active for some time, and I noticed that the Secretary of State


tabled a report on civil defence planning this morning. I have not, of course, had time to look at that report, but I shall be interested in doing so. The floods at Winnipeg and the fires at Rimouski and Cabano impressed upon all of us the desirability of having some sort of civilian defence set-up which could be used in such emergencies, quite apart from the extreme need for civilian defence in the event of war.
The minister said that the effective revival of the Hyde Park agreement had been advocated by Canada in order to enable the Canadian and United States forces to buy equipment from each other. I was glad to see an announcement in the press that some arrangement had been made which would enable the United States and Canadian forces to purchase from each other. Perhaps the minister can indicate what general types of equipment we shall produce in Canada and sell to the United States under that agreement, and what material we shall be purchasing from them.
We are being asked to vote large sums for defence. There is an amount of $425 million to be spent this year, but that is only part of the picture. So far as I can ascertain from a study of the estimates, there are further commitments amounting to nearly $200 million, so I think the total amount which we are being asked to vote for expenditures this year, or commitments in future years, is closer to $625 million rather than $425 million. In view of these large proposed expenditures this house should be given the fullest information as to how the money is to be spent, and particularly whether we are getting value for it. This involves, of course, being given information as to just what we are getting for the money expended; whether the expenditures will provide the defence necessary to look after this country, on a minimum scale of course. Everyone recognizes that it is impossible completely to defend this country, and no one dreams of advocating that. We should know whether the expenditures we are making are being made efficiently so as to provide this minimum force which the minister and the government have declared to be necessary. Now that this new concept has been adopted by the Atlantic pact nations, we should be told whether these expenditures are being made in such a way as to enable us effectively to play our part in carrying those plans forward.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the observations I shall make on the defence estimates I shall be speaking as an amateur. Indeed, I do not think there is anyone in the house today who can consider himself an expert on what our naval, military and air force

tactics of the future should be. I do not think we have a yardstick by which we can measure that.
I agree with what the hon. member for Calgary East had to say about the matter of expenditures. They should be broken down. We should have some idea as to what portion of our defence estimates are allocated for this, that or the other purpose. His whole talk this afternoon, however, to my mind was definitely based on war and not on defence.
As I see it, the objective of the United Nations, and the main objective of the North Atlantic pact, is to build machinery which would be ready to meet any potential aggressor; but that machinery is not being built for the purpose of carrying on a war. Its main purpose is the prevention of war. In discussing international affairs in matters of defence we have to be careful not to lend fuel to the propaganda machine that is operating both in the United States and in Canada, and largely throughout the world, and make it possible for anyone to say that we are engaged in an armaments race for the purpose of making war in the future rather than in efforts to prevent war. Our language will have to be temperate.
I am a bit disturbed myself about all the emphasis that is given these days to military matters, war, and the possibilities of war, and the slight attention that is paid to the only instrument, in my opinion, that can prevent war in the future, namely, the United Nations itself. From what I have been reading in the press and have been hearing in the discussions in the house in the last few days, my impression is that we are getting away completely from the United Nations as an instrument of preserving peace in the future; and in my opinion, that is the only body that can preserve it. Unless we can get together there, fully implement the terms of the United Nations charter, and negotiate and iron out around the conference table matters of international conflict, I believe that we are headed for something that we may not be able to control.
I do not think there is anyone inside or outside of this chamber who can offer a valid criticism of the North Atlantic pact. We accept it as an outgrowth of the United Nations. The United Nations charter provides for regional pacts where they are desirable and necessary; and there is at this time no doubt about the North Atlantic pact being necessary. It is a "must". But that machinery, so far, is in the embryo stage. There is nothing concrete that one can fasten on. They have had a meeting. They decided on certain economic and military commitments, but they are not definite. The principle is
Supply-National Defence right, and as such we shall have to support it and pay our share. Farther than that I am not prepared to go.
I think there are a great many difficulties in the world that we shall have to understand; for example, the situation in Germany. In my opinion it is the most explosive point in the world today. While the Russians are building peace fronts and talking about peace all over the world, in that particular section in Germany, in my opinion, they are building a war machine. They are now setting up a force consisting of 50,000 policemen. It is, in effect, an army, with tanks, artillery and all the rest of it. Canada should look at what the United States, Britain and France are doing in that particular sector and see what we can do to help in any way we can. As I say, I think that is the 'danger spot right now. Unless the situation is handled carefully and the difficulties are ironed out, there may be an eruption.
This afternoon what I want to focus the minister's attention on is not the broad matter of defence, because, as I said, most of us can fasten on to nothing that is concrete at the present time. The minister has nothing in history that he can use as a measure for the purpose of instructing his officials. I think if we vote the money, get an accounting of it as well as we can in the committee, and have some dependence on and confidence in those who are going to spend it and handle it in the future, with the minister as a contact between us and them, that is about all we can do at the present time.
What I want to talk to the minister about is a matter that we can do something about, and it has defence implications. In the house a few days ago I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question with regard to the naval air base at Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. According to press reports it is not in good shape. The Minister of Trade and Commerce at that time passed the question on to the Minister of Transport. The Minister of Transport took a look at it and said: "It belongs to the Minister of National Defence". I think that is one good argument for taking away from the governor in council some of the responsibility for decisions that can be passed around from one to the other, and for pinning it on someone specific. This particular question has to do with all three departments. I am going to talk about the part of it that comes within the scope of the Department of National Defence.
As the minister knows, in defence matters pertaining to Canada, Halifax area is a fairly strategic spot. It contributed greatly to the carrying on of the last two wars. The only airport in that whole area today is the one

Supply-National Defence at Dartmouth; and it is a naval airport. T.C.A. uses it for some small aircraft, the ones that they can land. The DC-3's I think are the only T.C.A. aircraft that can land there. The matter has been under discussion for over a year. The city of Halifax wanted to know from T.C.A. what they were going to do with regard to providing in that area facilities that could be used to land the North Star, for example, and put the port on the map from the standpoint of air service. The Minister of Trade and Commerce visited the area, and his opinion at that time, as expressed in the press, was to the effect that it would be better to spend a few million dollars expanding that naval station at Dartmouth so that it could be used for the dual purpose of defence for naval purposes and of providing T.C.A. facilities at that point. That was a year ago. Nothing has been done about it since. The question was raised again as late as the end of May of this year. The Halifax members were actively interested in it, according to press reports. An examination of the situation was made. For the minister's benefit I want to read something that was said by a member of the flying patrol division in that area. This is from the Halifax Mail-Star of May 25, and it is official; that is why I am going to read it. I quote:
Information about the present condition of the runways was offered by Lieutenant D. M. MacLeod, senior flying control at the Dartmouth naval station. "The runways are breaking up," he said. "Right now water is coming up through the tarmac, which is caused by the subgrade breaking down."
He said all four-engined aircraft were included in the 60,000-pound ban, with the possible exception of Lancasters. Constellations which have used the base from time to time have a gross weight of
74.000	pounds, and the United States strato-cruiser which landed there about a month ago weighed
120.000	pounds.	.
"The runways were originally built to handle
65.000	pounds," the lieutenant continued, "and the present ban is to prevent the runways from cracking up entirely."
If the runways were further damaged, a serious landing accident could occur, he said.
"It's to prevent this, and the cost of reconstructing new runways, that the ban has been placed in effect," he concluded.
The proposed weight ban would have no effect at present on Trans-Canada Air Lines operations out of Halifax, T.C.A. officials said.
At present T.C.A. are using the DC-3 passenger types which have a gross weight of 26,000 pounds when fully loaded.
That report from an official of the naval section paints a pretty bad picture of that particular station in Dartmouth. The runways are cracking up. Despite the fact that an active investigation has been carried on into the matter for the past year, so far nothing has been done with regard to expanding that Dartmouth station, or coming to the conclusion that a new station, particularly for the T.C.A. services, is to be established in
[Mr. Gillis.l

that section. I am afraid this is another indication of no thinking in the matter of services east of Montreal. Halifax is one of the major cities in this country. It has been used very extensively in both wars for defence purposes. Apparently both trade and commerce, T.C.A. and national defence have written off that area at this time because a couple of million dollars would have to be spent in building or expanding the service there.
There is a large number of personnel at that point; it is strategic in relation to the European continent and to Europe. So far as I can see now, there are no facilities and no thought of any in relation either to defence or to general services by air, in the minds of any of the officials of the government.
In view of the fact that the Department of National Defence proposes to spend $419,985,500 this year, and in view of the importance of that section and the condition of that particular airport, which is a defence airport, and the lack of thinking by other departments which have already expressed an opinion on the matter, I expect the Minister of National Defence to make a definite statement, before his estimates are carried, as to what he is going to do with the naval station in that particular section.
I should like to refer to the matter of recruiting. The hon. member for Calgary East said that the minister made a statement some time ago to the effect that they were getting all the recruits they needed in the services now. That may be true. But I think that with the standards they have in all three services today it is not so easy to get recruits, I have had a good many representations from boys who were in the services in the last war, who came out medically fit, who made a good contribution during their service, and who could not find employment after they got out of the service and who made application to go back in. They then had to take an educational test to get into any branch of the service, and they found they did not have the necessary basic education, and they could not get back in. If a war broke out these boys would be accepted.
During the last war, when an emergency hit us and we were in a hurry for recruits, we found that the physical condition of about forty-five per cent of those who tried to enlist was a pretty sorry indictment against us. In addition to that, from coast to coast there was such a high percentage of illiteracy among the young service personnel coming into the forces that the Department of National Defence was compelled to establish a school at North Bay where these young

boys were taken in and given a pretty thorough basic education in a short time. The whole curriculum was short-circuited in order to give them the necessary mechanics to understand map reading, gun laying and all that kind of thing. I suggest to the minister that one of the main defence preparations today should be an effort to see that our young people are qualified technically, and properly fed so that they will be physically fit when they come in.
The minister and his department should take another look at the number of applications that have come in from young men who want to get into the services but have been rejected because they have not the necessary basic education. Then, of course, we have to keep in mind the high percentage of young fellows who came out of the services at the end of the last war, but were not in a position to take advantage of even the vocational training supplied by the government because they did not have the necessary basic education. This is one matter that we should take a look at before we get into difficulties, because the condition of the world today is such that we cannot take chances. It may be too late to wait until you are hit in the nose before you start doing something about defending yourself. The general world condition, from the standpoint of possible war, is such that we should be building up the reserve army to the greatest extent possible. We should at least be giving, to those who desire to take it, the necessary basic training so that in the event of an emergency, they will be called in with some knowledge of what is expected of them.
I think the policy adopted by the department shortly after the war is the correct one. They are building up a hard corps of well-trained personnel. They are keeping them in camps at strategic spots across the country. That is all to the good. That is what should be done at this time. In addition, emphasis should be placed on the reserve army, to see that in the event of an emergency, as many as possible have the necessary basic education in military matters. Next time it may be a matter of having to defend yourself, whether you like it or not. Everyone who is thinking at all will agree that if another war breaks out we shall be the Belgium of that war. It will not be a matter of going thousands of miles to get into the fight. You may find yourself in it overnight.
As I said, we hope that the formation of the North Atlantic pact, along with co-operation in economic and military spheres, tied in with whatever efforts we can make through the United Nations to fight to the last ditch in preserving peace-if that is possible-will keep the peace. If it is not possible, and we 55046-213
Supply-National Defence are forced into war by an act of aggression by the only country in the world today that is in a position to commit an act of aggression, then everyone in the country should be prepared to understand that situation and should be equipped so that we may be able to make the best possible fight under any circumstances.	.	.
My particular reason for rising was not to lecture the minister. I am prepared to pass these estimates. I have met some of the officials of the Department of National Defence. In those I have met I have confidence. The minister is here to be questioned at any time, and I think most of us have confidence in his ability and integrity. I rose this afternoon only to focus his attention on something concerning which he can take action; I refer to the naval station at Dartmouth.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take this opportunity to draw to the attention of the minister and the committee some matters in connection with the Department of National Defence which, I think, should receive some consideration. The point I am about to raise is one which affects not only this department but some other departments of government as well.
I have been interested in the case of a young airman whose name, for obvious reasons, I should prefer not to give. This young man was dismissed from the air force some time ago, apparently because of some charges made against him to the effect that at some time during his earlier life he had been connected with the communist party.
It so happens that I have known of this family for about forty years. It is a Roman Catholic family living in the province of Saskatchewan. The young lad to whom I refer was for a time a student in a Roman Catholic institution. That in itself is something by way of background that should reinforce what I am going to say. After serving several years in the R.C.A.F. this young man was suddenly let out-and he was let out under a cloud. He has never seen any charge made against him, and therefore has never been given an opportunity to endeavour to refute such charge.
So far as I am able to understand, some thirteen or fourteen years ago, during the period of unemployment, when protest meetings of all kinds were being held across the country, this young man attended a meeting -perhaps it was two meetings-in Regina of unemployed young men. When he discovered that the purpose of the meetings was to recruit young men for service in Spain, and to join the communist party as it was then, he went home and had nothing further to do with the matter. So far as I

Supply-National Defence have been able to find out that is the only action that gave rise to suspicion concerning his associations. I know of no other.
1 may add that Mr. Douglas, premier of Saskatchewan, has been acquainted with the family for the last twenty years, and perhaps has seen this lad and the other members of his family more recently than I have. But the point I make is this, that when any person in any public service is placed under a cloud and under suspicion, in a democratic country he should at least have the opportunity of knowing what the charges are against him. My criticism of the department is that, in this case, although they have been asked to state what the charge was, this has never been done and, so far as I know, no one has been given access to any of the information.
I have been keenly interested in the case and have gone so far as to suggest that if I could be given an opportunity to see the evidence and to be satisfied in my own mind, I was quite sure I could satisfy Mr. Douglas and that I could either give my word that the dismissal was deserved or, if it was not, ask the minister to look into the matter further. I know that even during wartime, when matters of a confidential nature arose concerning men in the air force, the minister's predecessors-and I am thinking particularly of the former minister for air-had no hesitation in trying to satisfy any member of parliament who was interested in a case that the action taken had been fully justified, and that there had been good reasons for taking it.
I have known the minister for a number of years. I have known him to be most insistent upon civil liberties, and it has been most difficult for me indeed to understand how this could happen under the minister's administration. I rise this afternoon not only in the interests of one young man who may or may not be guilty, and who may or may not have deserved dismissal from the armed forces. I raise the matter because, speaking generally, there is no opportunity in other departments for an accused employee to have a review of the accusations made against him.
We pride ourselves on our democratic traditions, and on the fact that to a large extent our parliamentary institutions are a reflection of the age-old institution of parliament in the United Kingdom. There a most careful screening is made, although mistakes occasionally do occur. However, when an individual is charged the minister receives advice from a competent and trustworthy committee to which the accused may appeal. While the committee has no power to reinstate or to take other remedial action, it can advise the


minister who, of course, takes the final responsibility. There is a method of review and appeal. I suggest to the government, not only to the Department of National Defence in which the particular case I have mentioned falls, but to the government in general, that in cases of this kind there should be an opportunity for an individual to clear his name, if he can.
After all, it seems to me that an accusation of this description places a man under a cloud and makes it difficult for him to find other suitable employment. The young man to whom I am referring was at the beginning of last month among the unemployed and, because of a lack of references and because of inability to explain properly why he had been let out, had been unable to get employment of a kind suited to his particular talents. I am bringing this to the attention of the committee and I do not think anyone who knows my point of view will misunderstand why I bring it to the floor of parliament.
Under the present circumstances I think the government has to be wary. Where you have within the country a political movement that is the agency of a foreign power you cannot be too careful, but in exercising that care equal care should be taken that no injustice is done to any individual. Under our traditional democratic rights, according to our idea of justice, a person who is accused should have at least the opportunity of knowing something of the accusation against him and be given opportunity to review that accusation.

Mr. Chairman, in taking part
