Supply-National Defence And again:
"No sane man will challenge under the present circumstances the need for defensive strength designed to secure against internal or external attack the independence and sovereignty of a free state," he added. "But the continued existence of even one purely defensive force-a force of which there is no apparent need based in the logic of self defence-denies enduring peace to the world.
Those who have spawned such a force must either eventually destroy it by demobilization and find justification for the heavy cost already laid upon their people; or use it, tacitly or actively, as a threat or as a weapon. There is no middle course."
It is sad to think that after two terrible wars fought for the preservation of our free way of life we have to spend $425 million or more this year on our armed services which could be spent much more profitably in developing our great natural resources for the betterment of the people of this country and of all mankind. To such a state has this world now come. Truly it can be said, "Those whom the gods would destroy they first make mad." The honourable and gallant member for Nanaimo has spoken of the differences that exist in the higher command regarding which branch of the services needs priority of development. It is fitting that this should be brought to the attention of the house, and I do not propose to question the hon. member as to the source of his information. This difference of opinion amongst the higher command is not new. Those who have read military history know that such things have existed in all ages. In recent months we have had the spectacle of bitter differences of opinion between the United States navy and air force over which arm of the services will be most effective in modern warfare, and this wordy warfare still continues. It would be strange indeed if something of this struggle did not affect the thinking of Canada's higher command.
Therefore I am not unduly alarmed at such differences of opinion provided these officers are imbued with a high sense of their responsibilities, which I believe they possess, and their differences are animated by a sincere desire to serve the best interests of their country.
Since we evidently cannot develop all our services sufficiently to meet all our requirements, it may be necessary to give priority to one branch. This must be done by taking all the factors of defence into consideration. For myself I favour the air arm of the services for the following reasons: To those who have studied the lessons of the last war it must be evident that without air superiority armies are very seriously handicapped. It was the German command of the air that caused Poland to collapse so quickly. It was the same in the German break through
[Mr. Stick.l
to the channel ports. It was the German air force that captured Crete. It was this same force that prepared the way for the German armies in their advance into Russia, and it was only after the Russian air force became at least equal to the enemy air force that we saw the tide of war turn in that country. We would never have landed successfully in Normandy without command of the air, and it was that same superiority that made the break through possible.
It is the same story in sea warfare. It was the Japanese air force that first attacked Pearl Harbor and sank two of Britain's battleships in the China sea. It was the air arm that, unaided, found and crippled the Bismarck. The whole story of the United States naval victories in the Pacific is the story of the naval air arm destroying Japanese fleets almost single-handed. It was the air arm that played a large share in crushing the U-boat menace. I think I have said enough to show why our air force must be developed at all costs. Finally the lessons of Exercise Sweetbriar show that without proper air support you cannot fight successfully in the Arctic.
According to the latest reliable reports Russia has at least 300 modern submarines of the very latest design. When we consider that the Germans began the last war with about 60 submarines, and the great destruction they caused our shipping, the menace from this type of warfare becomes evident. That this is so recognized is demonstrated by the fact that the United States navy is pursuing antisubmarine measures with all possible speed and giving priority to them. We in Newfoundland know a good deal about what submarines can do. Our experience during the last war is not one we wish repeated. I am glad therefore to note that the Department of National Defence recognizes this danger and is building three ships specially designed for antisubmarine work.
It is pleasing to note that recruiting in Newfoundland is going ahead with excellent results. It is especially gratifying to know that the Royal Newfoundland Regiment has been reconstituted and incorporated into the Canadian reserve army. Without in any way boasting, but speaking purely from the record, I should like to tell the house that in Newfoundland we have some of the finest fighting material in the world, whether on sea, land, or in the air.
The times in which we live demand a strong defensive force, and if we are to maintain it in the highest degree of efficiency we have to Show our young men that we are solidly behind them in every reasonable way. One of the greatest soldiers of all ages laid

down as an axiom of war that morale is to the physical as three to one. If we are to carry out this great principle we must demonstrate our complete confidence in our armed forces. In this way we can do our part in building that morale which is so essential to any branch of the armed services. Finally I wish to say that the position Newfoundland holds is vital to the defence not only of Canada but of a large part of the North American continent. Canada must also play her part in that defence. Truly it can be said of Newfoundland, in the words of our national anthem, "O Canada, we stand on guard for thee".

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
In taking part in this debate I should like to limit my few remarks to the present policy of the department in relation to the naval service. During the last war the navy rendered tremendous service to the allied cause. For a while we had the third largest navy in the world, and we had what was then regarded as the best antisubmarine service in all the allied forces. At that time there were 90,000 men in the navy. They were well trained, and we had the equipment to do the job. It was strictly an antisubmarine navy. That was then regarded as the proper policy for the navy, and I think the situation has not changed much as we can see from the various press reports and other information we get about our potential enemy.
We see that at the present time Russia has more fast and well equipped submarines than Germany had before the last war. Therefore it is only natural that we should look to our navy from the point of view of antisubmarine defence, and that we should do everything to make sure that it is an effective weapon in that regard. Unfortunately I think we are not spending the taxpayers' money, so far as the navy is concerned, in the best way we could. At the present time we have one aircraft carrier. It is costing a lot of money for upkeep and necessitates a fleet air arm with proper training stations, equipment and aircraft which are very expensive, and most of which are obsolete. At the same time we have in operation, so far as A.S. ships are concerned, only seven destroyers and four frigates. When an aircraft carrier is at sea during wartime such a ship has to be escorted by destroyers. If there were a war tomorrow one of our coasts would be defended by an aircraft carrier with three or four or five destroyers escorting her. At the same time the other coast would be defended by four or five A.S. ships. A few Russian submarines could attack our shipping lanes, and even our harbours, without much difficulty. In my opinion the money
Supply-National Defence we are spending for a single aircraft carrier is not wisely spent, when one considers that for the same amount of money we could have more fast destroyers, and fast well-equipped A.S. ships, to fight submarines. These vessels could defend both the Atlantic and the Pacific coast lines at the same time, and we would not be in the position where a single torpedo could put half of our navy out of action. I believe this matter should be seriously studied by the department. I hope the minister will keep in mind the tremendous sum of money that has been spent for our single aircraft carrier, and I hope the navy will give careful consideration to these A.S. ships, which would be of vital importance if a war developed between Canada and Russia.
One other point I might draw to the attention of this house and the minister is that the parliamentary assistant to the minister replied to a question by the member for Nanaimo by stating that the cost of keeping up our single aircraft carrier in 1949 amounted to $2,940,000. For the two carrier groups, it amounted to $1,577,000, making a grand total for the carrier operation of $4,500,000. For the same amount I think Canada could maintain a fleet of fast and efficient antisubmarine ships which would give better protection to our shipping lanes.
One other point which strikes me, and I think this house should know about it, is that while the parliamentary assistant was giving this grand total for carrier operations of $4,500,000, the naval chief of staff was in Vancouver. According to a Canadian Press report he stated that the maintenance cost of the aircraft carrier H.M.C.S. Magnificent and the navy air arm was about $20 million per year. If the air arm is costing us $20 million, it could mean that we could afford to have even more A.S. ships than if the cost were the lower figure given by the parliamentary assistant, which was only about one-quarter of that mentioned by the chief of staff. We would still be able to do a more efficient job so far as the defence of Canada is concerned. If we decide to have these small A.S. ships, they can be built in Canada. In this way we could help our Canadian shipyards, which did such a tremendous amount of work during the last war, and which have been left high and dry since the end of the war. I believe it would be a good way to defend our coasts, and a good way to spend the taxpayers' money. It would also be a good way to help our Canadian shipyards.
These are a few of the remarks I wanted to make, and I hope the minister will explain to us why there is this apparent discrepancy

Supply-National Defence between the $4,500,000 that his department gave as the maintenance cost of our air arm, and the $20 million that the naval chief of staff says it is costing.

Under the recent decisions made at the North Atlantic council meeting in London, as indicated by the communique which the minister read to the house some time ago, a permanent deputy was to be chosen by Canada to attend the continued discussions of that council. Can the minister indicate who that permanent deputy is going to be, and, if he is not able to do that, when we may expect the appointment to be announced?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am sure the committee will appreciate that any member discussing national defence at' the present time can only do so on the basis of his own information, and it is extremely difficult to form any sound opinions in view of the extremely rapid changes which appear to be taking place in the over-all picture of defence policy, particularly with relation to the Atlantic pact conference in London. I am sure the minister will appreciate also that in the remarks which I, at any rate, will make this afternoon, although it is difficult to discuss matters of this kind and not to make a statement that at least appears dogmatic, whatever the result may be I am not trying to criticize his department but desire to secure an understanding of what our policy is. As I said, I do not wish to be critical, but I must say that I for one find it most difficult to get a clear picture of our defence policy, or whether any decision has yet been made as to the over-all constitution of our forces and the clear role which they are to fulfil, particularly with respect to joint Atlantic defence. It has not been made clear yet whether we are able to outline a policy of building up forces in accordance with a set design which is clearly formulated in the minds of defence officials. It is the answer to those questions which has been concerning me, and the questions which are raised by that consideration which I should like to discuss.
In approaching the matter this afternoon I s,hall confine my remarks mainly to an attempted analysis of the statements made from time to time by the minister and suggestions as to what it seems to me those statements mean, in the hope that if my analysis


is wrong the minister will correct me and that, in the process, we can get some indication of what our policy is. In his statement made on March 17 this year, when he introduced his estimates, the minister dealt first with the meetings of the Atlantic pact countries. At page 851 of Hansard he is reported to have made the following statement:
The defence committee meeting at Paris received reports on this work and arrived at unanimous agreement on the following:
1.	A strategic concept for the integrated defence of the north Atlantic area.
2.	The means to be taken to arrive at a program for the production and supply of armament and equipment.
3.	Co-ordination of planning between the various regional groups.
4.	Additional steps to further defence planning of the North Atlantic treaty organization.
Then he went on:
Since the Paris meetings, further action has been taken in the various regional groups.
As the minister himself pointed out in the course of the next few paragraphs, work in the north Atlantic group was being continued permanently and further meetings were taking place later that month. He himself left during the month of March for meetings of the military committee and the defence committee at The Hague on March 24, 27 and April 1 respectively. Those meetings were held subsequent to the minister's statement, and I should like to ask him whether he is able to tell us what has been done with reference to the four headings he gave us on which he said unanimous agreement has been reached.
As I read them, those four statements are merely over-all statements of policy. What I should like to know is whether the defence committee of the Atlantic pact nations has been able to agree on any concrete measures by means of which to apply its policy; and particularly I should like to know if the minister can tell us in at least a general way what has been done to implement the decision he has referred to under item 2, namely, the means to be taken to arrive at a program for the production and supply of armament and equipment. It certainly appears that one of the most important decisions to be taken and then to be implemented is on this question of the unification of our arms production program. If the minister was able to say in March that agreement had been reached at that time on the means to be taken to work out a program for the production and supply of armament and equipment, I hope that he can tell us now what steps have been taken as a result of that decision.
On several occasions the minister has told us in the house that Canada has not yet

accepted any formal commitment under the North Atlantic pact and therefore that he could not tell the house what was the role of our armed forces with respect to the pact. He has also, however, told us on several occasions the role of the various elements of our forces with regard to domestic defence. I hope that he can now perhaps carry the picture a little bit further forward and take us with him in telling us whether, as a result of those meetings at The Hague and the recent meetings in London, we are any closer to getting a picture of what is to be Canada's role under the integrated defence program of the Atlantic nations.
I refer there, of course, particularly to the communique issued after the London meeting and referred to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs the other day, when it was said that a decision had been arrived at to the effect that rather than each country of the pact having its own completely balanced forces of army, navy and air force, there should be joint balanced forces, with each of the member nations contributing that portion of the forces which its own position best qualified it to contribute. I am wondering therefore whether the minister can tell us whether any decision has been reached with respect to this country, as to what part of the joint Atlantic community defence forces will be Canada's main contribution. I use the phrase "defence forces". I realize that it might possibly be held that Canada's main contribution is not in the way of armed forces alone but rather in the way of armament, equipment and research. But I am using the phrase, in asking what contribution Canada is to make to the joint defence forces, I hope in a sense broad enough to include the question of armament production and research.
Coming to the question of immediate domestic defence, I should like to ask the minister whether he can give us any assurance or reassurance about what is being done to provide adequate defence for Canada's Pacific coast. The hon. member for Nanaimo -I realize that his opinion may not be fully shared by the minister, but I certainly do not hesitate to quote it as a qualified opinion- has stated in debate on this subject in recent years that there was a large defence gap on the Pacific coast, and that that defence gap consisted of Canada's British Columbia coast. I do not think that the point raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo at that time was fully or completely answered by any of the statements made since. The remarks just made by the hon. member for Three Rivers seemed to me to reinforce the argument which the hon. member for Nanaimo had advanced
Supply-National Defence on previous occasions. In his statement on March 17 the minister gave us the present composition of our naval forces. This may be found at page 859 of Hansard. He stated:
In the R.C.N. we shall have in commission on the west coast the cruiser Ontario; the destroyers Atha-baskan, Cayuga and Siotix; the frigate Antigonish; the Algerine escort vessels Rockcliffe and Sault Ste. Marie; the auxiliary vessel CedarwoocL; and the patrol craft 724.
On the east coast we will have the aircraft carrier Magnificent; the destroyers Micmac, Huron and Haida; the weather ship St. Stephen; the frigate Swansea; the Algerine minesweeping vessel Portage; and the motor minesweeper Llewellyn.
In looking over that picture, it seems to me it is obvious that the naval force on the Atlantic coast is a much more integrated force-and I hope I shall not offend any of my friends of the navy because I realize that I am not familiar with naval terminology.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: You are doing very well.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
It seems to me that it is a much more integrated task force, if that is the correct word, or potential task force than we have on the Pacific coast.
Again to refer to this question of antisubmarine work, my understanding of it is this, although I must confess it has been to some extent shaken at any rate by what the hon. member for Three Rivers has just said. My understanding of the current theory with respect to antisubmarine naval requirements was that the force was built largely around an aircraft carrier, and that the naval aircraft from this carrier did a large part, if not the main part, of the work of spotting the submarines which were to be destroyed. If I am at all correct in that understanding, it would seem to me that we have at least the elements of a composite antisubmarine task force in our Atlantic naval units, but we have not the necessary elements, or hardly any of the necessary elements, on the Pacific coast. Therefore I come back to the question, do we intend to close that gap with respect to our defences on the Pacific, to which the hon. member for Nanaimo referred?
In his review of our domestic defence program the minister did point out that we were doing very much indeed to integrate the active army brigade groups and the active air force training, particularly with respect to northern defence; that we had made great progress in that direction, as shown by Exercise Sweet-briar. Well, no one should in any sense suggest that we should pay less attention to that aspect of our defence program, but I hope I may be allowed to lay before the minister as strongly as I possibly can the suggestion that we on the Pacific coast certainly feel

Supply-National Defence that our defences in that region should not be neglected entirely as the result of an exclusive or over-emphatic concentration on northern and Arctic defences. I should like therefore to raise the question of the defence of our own installations in the Pacific area.
As the committee may know, the three main ammunition depots on the Pacific coast are in the vicinity of the city of Kamloops. We have the air force depot, the naval magazine depot and the army ordnance and ammunition depot. These are three very considerable establishments. The naval one particularly, I believe, is the largest of its kind in Canada. It does occur to me that in the event of hostilities these would be very likely targets of an attack on Canada. I should like the minister to indicate to us, if he can, without going further than he wishes for security reasons, as a part of the approach to the Pacific defence, what steps or plans are taken in the department for the defence of these three depots.
Dealing particularly with the role of the army in the domestic defence picture, the minister said, as it is reported on page 859 of Hansard of March 17:
The role of the army is equally clear. It is to provide the forces necessary to meet an immediate attack on our country any time and any place. To do this we have organized a brigade group, a highly mobile, hard-hitting unit. More than half of this group consists today of well-trained, experienced, tough soldiers.
I am sure that all hon. members were very glad indeed to hear the minister report that progress made in the training and equipment of our brigade group; but I am reasonably confident that the minister will agree with me that, although this brigade group may be able, as he said, to fill the role which he himself laid down for it, namely, to provide the forces necessary to meet an immediate attack on our country any time and any place, yet it is not sufficient of itself to meet more than one initial attack, and that if the initial attack were multiplied, if it should come in more localities than one, then by its very nature a brigade group would not be able to deal with a diversified and sustained attack. Therefore I hope the minister will agree with me that in so far as Canada's own forces are concerned, to meet that type of attack

and I fully realize that in the event of a large-scale attack we will have to rely on, and would certainly receive the support of, the United States-in considering this problem from the viewpoint of Canada, it becomes obvious that in meeting, ourselves, any large-scale and diversified attack we do need a highly trained and immediately available reserve force in addition to that mobile permanent force brigade group.


Therefore I should like to refer to what the minister himself said on page 859 in analysing further the role of the army. He said:
In addition to seeing to the immediate defence of our own territory, our forces must act as the organizational and training nucleus for the development of the largest forces we can develop to play our part where they may be needed. A large part of the personnel of the army-all the reserve units and a very large portion, certainly more than two-thirds of the active forces-are concerned with this side of the job.
I would like the minister, if he can, to give us a statement on the state of preparation, the state of manning and training of the reserve army. This may be an exaggerated concept that I am about to put forward, but I think it is the sort of thing we should work toward. That is, that the reserve army should not be the type of reserve army we have had in the past, and I am in no sense attaching any blame to anybody in what I say here. The picture has changed. But I do not think the type of reserve army we have had in the past meets the requirements of today at all. I visualize our requirements as calling for a reserve force in which almost literally every man has his number and his place in the unit and, as it were, his place in the barracks, in stores, and has a rifle and complete equipment, so that the procedure of mobilizing a reserve army and of fielding at least an initial reserve force would not be one of six months but rather of six- I was going to say six weeks or six days- that within a matter of days we would know where each man was to complete a unit, and that each man would have his own equipment allocated so that the man and the equipment could be conjoined immediately and the forces fielded. I realize that is easy to say but difficult to accomplish. I realize too it may involve a higher degree of training for our reserve army, but I hope not a higher degree of training than I visualize.
I should like the minister to make a statement on the present status of the manning, training and equipment of our reserve army, and what program is in mind for bringing that reserve army up to that category of an immediately available field force.
I should like to refer to some of the implications, on the broader basis, of the statement made recently by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and in the communique issued following the Atlantic pact meetings in London. Here of course one does get very much into the realm of the uncertain. But the impact of these statements on the thinking of the people of this country has been very considerable. On the one hand, we hear some who suggest that what was done at the Atlantic pact meeting was not more than a

statement of broad general principles of no immediate application. But on the other hand there are those who say, and with a good deal of foundation for their statement, that the decisions taken at the Atlantic pact meeting involved an immediate and very substantial change, or necessity for a change, in our defence policy. If the committee will indulge me I should like to read at some length from a Canadian Press article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of June 7, the day following the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this house. The Canadian Press reporter says:
Atlantic pact arms developments in the next few years hold a strong possibility of working big changes in Canada's forces and in plans to send overseas a third expeditionary force mainly composed of infantry in any new war, informed quarters said today.
Within five years, they said, the use of massed infantry could easily be obsolete. Such military efforts as the tight, tough land battles in Italy and the D-day landings in Normandy would be ruled out by the violence of mass destruction weapons.
This trend is of obvious and vital importance in view of Russia's stress on land forces, her almost unlimited ability to reinforce them and her relative immaturity in the scientific and technical fields.
Then the article continues:
Defence officials here-
And this carries a dateline at Ottawa, June 6.
-said scientific advances now are moving towards push-button warfare at a pace which has defence headquarters constantly examining plans and revamping them.
Canada's plans to contribute are largely secret but may, it was learned, lead to loan of scientists, to work on guided missiles and rockets and to use of remote Canadian soil as ranges for testing those developed by Canada or her allies. Some secret projects now are on Ottawa drawing boards.
Then, skipping one or two paragraphs, the article continues:
Mr. Pearson said yesterday the pact's acceptance of the principle of balanced collective forces may mean new applications of scientific warfare and "abandonment of the old concept of defence by great masses of infantry . .
And later:
It doesn't mean that Canada would definitely not send another expeditionary force overseas. It does mean, however, that the proportion of infantry in any overseas force would be considerably less than before. In their stead would be the skilled technicians who handle rockets and missiles. The infantry division, as such, might vanish or be sharply altered.
The last paragraph states:
It is a "reasonable assumption," a reporter was told, that for the first time a new war would not be started the way the last one ended. The infantry's relative importance would drop and there would be a larger proportion of manpower dispatching mass destruction weapons.
Supply-National Defence
If one examines this in relation to the minister's statement of March 17, I think several questions arise. I am not suggesting that the statements in this article must be taken as a statement of defence policy, although I do point out that it is a Canadian Press article, refers to government sources and statements of defence officials, and that the article originates in Ottawa. On March 17, as reported at page 856 of Hansard, the minister said:
Our planning must look several years ahead. On the one hand we must start work in time to produce the results in personnel and equipment when they are likely to be needed. On the other hand, we must avoid starting things now which might involve us in future commitments for the expenditure of money which might then be needed for other defence purposes of greater priority.
One may recall that only a couple of years ago in discussions on defence matters it was indicated by the minister, and such other statements of defence policy as were made, that the thinking of the department was to the effect that we should not commit ourselves at the present time to any definite form of armed services, that is to say to any permanent division of effort as between the three services, nor should we commit ourselves to any permanent line of equipment for fear that we might embark upon programs which would be obsolete, or at least obsolescent in a couple of years, when perhaps an emergency might arise and we would need those forces and equipment.
When one remembers that that was the defence policy only two years ago-and I believe it was the same last year-then in the light of the statement to which I have just referred I think a very definite question arises as to what has brought about the change of policy, and the present policy in the department which places such great emphasis upon the expenditure of money for the acquisition of equipment as though- and I think this is the only inference that can be drawn-we have now decided what will be the design of our forces and what basic equipment-indeed,*in some cases what detailed equipment-we shall go in for.
I recall that only two years ago it was indicated that defence thinking was that there would be no war in the immediate future as a result of deliberate planning, that no country was contemplating waging a deliberate war, that we need not contemplate such an event for at least ten years, but that with the various tension spots around the world such as Berlin-it was the main one at that time, and perhaps still is-and with the various encroachments of communist imperialism in one country after another

Supply-National Defence new tensions might arise, that there might be an explosion and that a war might result more or less accidentally.
The theory was that such accidental war would be lought generally along the same lines as the one just concluded. There would be certain developments of certain techniques which would be carried to further perfection as a result of the last war, but that generally speaking such accidental war in the few years immediately ahead would be along the lines of the last one. It was urged therefore that we should not make too early a decision as to new techniques, new weapons and new formations which would form a permanent design for our defence forces. It was felt that their use would not be likely until the development of something more deliberate, and that such could not take place until some ten years in the future.
What has caused the change in emphasis? What has brought about the change in policy in the Department of National Defence which results in the emphasis now being placed upon the purchase of equipment? Let me point out that so definite was the earlier policy that we should not begin too soon to build up a permanent design for our forces and equipment that there was indeed a good deal of criticism. I am sure the minister is used to criticism, and that he is particularly used to it when it comes from the source from which I am now about to quote, But the point I wish to establish is that the policy to which I have been referring, a policy of wait and see, was so firmly established and maintained that considerable criticism resulted therefrom in the newspapers, in the press, and indeed in the House of Commons.
The Montreal Gazette, of March 17, 1948, carried an editorial in which it pointed out the danger of too rigid adherence to the policy of wait and see. This editorial is headed "Small But Efficient". I believe some of the principles laid down in the editorial are so sound that it might be well to place them before the committed at this time. Referring to the fact that in the view of this writer the insistence upon a policy of wait and see resulted in inefficiency in the design of our forces, because the men were not being equipped with what they should have, and because the very purpose and design of the forces was not clearly laid down, the writer had this to say:
This is not to say that the inefficiency of the forces comes about from their own failure to make the most of the opportunities that have been provided for them. But it does appear that they are not being furnished with every chance to attain true efficiency. For the only real test of efficiency in modern war is the adequacy of the new means to the new ends. It seems that since 1945 very few

new weapons have been provided to keep training in close relations with a rapidly developing reality. Some of the hesitation in providing the modern equipment would seem to come about from a chronic sense that something a little newer and better may be just around the comer. This feeling is well founded, as no weapon, however new, will ever remain unimproved.
Then continuing:
But the hesitation in providing modern equipment would seem to have deeper causes. There are evidences of a lack of decision as to just what purpose our armed forces are supposed to serve. Are we to have an offensive or a defensive force? Which of the three armed services is considered to be of paramount importance? Is our primary aim to defend our own borders from attack? With which of our allies is the co-ordination of our arms most important?
And finally:
The idea of a small and efficient force, if it is to be stated at all, could be stated as that of a "small but efficient force." The efficiency, in short, is the only justification of the smallness. There is no virtue or value in smallness as such. And yet there appears to be a very real danger that the smallness will be left to itself. And, from the figures, it seems that even that will be very small indeed.
I have read that to show that only two years ago the emphasis, in so far as it could be gathered from the statements by the minister and others in the defence department, was on "wait and see." The idea seemed to be that no deliberate war-if I may use that word-was likely for at least several years, perhaps up to ten, and therefore we should not go too fast in laying down a permanent design for our forces and adopting permanent equipment with which they would be finally armed.
Now the emphasis is all on bringing our requirements up to need, on equipping or catching up with the backlog of equipment for the forces which we have in existence. On several occasions in March the minister referred to the heavy proportion of our defence expenditures which was going to equipment, and I quote from page 852 of Hansard of March 17, 1950, where the minister is reported as follows:
The greatest shortage is equipment as other commitments have so far prevented much production in quantity. We appear-
I am adding the word "now":

now to be spending in proportion more on equipment than the other countries.
And then I quote from page 856 as follows:
In 1948, 12 per cent of the total appropriation was spent on equipment; in 1949, 24 per cent and in the coming year it will be 28 per cent. This trend reflects both the increasing cost of fighting machines and the importance which is attached to having up to date weapons in the hands of our services. It is, I am sure hon. members will agree, a desirable and proper approach.

In other statements the minister has made reference to the fact that the reason why our defence spending is as heavy as it is now is in large part the fact we are spending so largely on equipment. 1 should like to ask now why there has been what can be described only as a change in policy. Is there any change in the approach of the department to the concept of our defence requirements or the dangers which we face and which make necessary this change in policy in so far as equipment is concerned? Are we closer to an actual threat than was thought to be the case only two years ago when the other policy was formulated?
There are just one or two particular matters I want to refer to before I conclude and these arise out of the fact that we are spending so heavily on equipment. The hon. member for Nanaimo has referred already to the dangers inherent in our heavy commitments with respect to the purchase and construction of the United States jet fighter, the F-86. On March 17 the hon. member made this statement as reported on page 863 of Hansard:
The proposed production program which I understand, according to press reports, will see the F-86 coming into production either at the end of this year or in 1951, raises serious doubts in my mind as to whether it will not be an obsolescent machine before it comes off the line. These doubts are reinforced by the decision which I understand has been taken in the United States in which orders for an improved type of Sabre, the F-93, have been cancelled. Doubts have been expressed in leading aviation papers in the United States that the F-86 will ever become a practical interceptor. I do suggest that money should have been saved to this country if the R.C.A.F. had continued to use the improved Vampire types during the interim until our own CF-100 becomes generally available, which I gather, from the remarks made by the minister this afternoon, will be toward next year.
The grave doubts cast by the hon. member for Nanaimo in his well-founded statement on the wisdom of equipping ourselves with F-86 machines has not yet been cleared up by the minister. In view of the current emphasis on uniformity in arms production it seems to me that those doubts are further accentuated, particularly when we understand that the United States now regard this particular jet as obsolete. Is Canada to be the only country using this fighter while the United Kingdom and other Atlantic pact countries, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Nanaimo, are adopting the use of the British Vampire and Venom machines, of which we already have the basic type here? It does seem to me that we are making a mistake in adopting the United States F-86 instead of using the up-to-date British jet fighters until our own are ready for delivery in Canada.

I do not think so. The final
question I wish to raise is being raised at this time because it concerns large numbers of people in this country. First I should like the minister to state whether the Canadian war graves in Europe come under his department?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: They would be under defence.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
On the permanent headstones and crosses of the graves of Canadian soldiers who died in the last war there is no reference to the unit to which they belonged. This matter has been referred to before in a question and answer on the order paper. I am sure that other hon. members as well as myself have received reports about this from former members of the forces who have visited the graves of relatives or friends, as well as from relatives of soldiers who are buried overseas. The Canadian graves seem to be the only ones where no mention of the unit is made on the headstone or cross. Some of these reports have been couched in quite strong language. I am not going to use the same language because it seems to me that this is a matter which is bound to cause distress to the relatives of those who are buried there. Therefore I think the more moderately one can discuss the matter the better. My feelings are very strong. I do not really see any justification or reason for the identity of the soldier not being preserved, and it is regarded by those who served in the units that their identity existed-I will not say was submerged-with that of the other members of the unit with whom they served. It is only proper and fitting that such identity should be preserved on the headstone memorial marking their last resting place. It is a matter which I know has caused grave distress to many of the relatives in Canada.
I make no apologies for bringing it up at this time although, as I say, I am going to deal with it in as moderate language as I can. Nevertheless I say to the minister that I feel very strongly about it, and I know I represent the views of many others who feel equally strongly that there is no good reason or justification for it, and that the policy

Supply-National Defence should be immediately reversed. Those who go to the burial grounds of Canadian soldiers overseas know so well the traditions, ideals, fortunes and adversities which their relatives shared with their fellow members of the same unit. The first question they ask is: Where are the members of the Edmonton regiment? They look for some reference to the regiment to assist them to find the burial place of their own relatives. It comes as a distinct and distressing shock to them to find that no reference to the unit is embodied on the memorial stones.
I think the minister should, and I hope he will, review the policy and change it so that the name of the unit may be carved on the headstones marking the last resting place of those Canadians who fought with and were proud of their units. A nominal roll by units of those who rest there should also be preserved in the records of the graves.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Perhaps first of all I might say to the minister that I am not one of those who agree with the point of view expressed earlier this afternoon by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres concerning the fleet air arm of the Royal Canadian Navy. It is true that the operation of our aircraft carrier and the fleet air arm generally is expensive. Looking at it from that point of view alone, it is perhaps not too difficult to conclude that there might be some justification for a reduction of the expenses involved in the operation of that service. I think, however, that point of view does not take into consideration the development of operations and policies in naval services throughout the world, and the particular role that the Canadian navy will be called upon to play in any future hostilities. In spite of the fact that it is expensive I think we must keep a naval air arm and provide it with adequate facilities and the necessary equipment and training to maintain it as an efficient fighting force.
Consideration of naval air policy brings me to the main reason for my saying anything this afternoon on the defence estimates. I wish to refer to a problem dealt with earlier by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the airport facilities at Eastern Passage, Halifax county. The airport at Eastern Passage is the main operational and training base for the fleet air arm, and is known as H.M.C.S. Shearwater. Everyone will fully appreciate that as a military base the Department of National Defence must see that it is an efficient operation, that its facilities are what are required for the immediate purposes of the service, and that its utility to the service is not unreasonably affected by any other consideration.


I should like to point out to the minister that ever since this airport was constructed at Eastern Passage as an air base for the R.C.A.F., it has also been used as the only civilian airport serving Halifax and the whole of the central section of the province of Nova Scotia. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the Department of National Defence must take into consideration the use of that airport for civilian purposes ever since it was brought into operation. Turning for a moment to the use of the airport for military or naval purposes, I should like to point out to the minister that, while the airport may be suitable for the main use to which it is being put at the present time by the naval air service, the landing of carrier aircraft, it is an unavoidable conclusion that developments in military and naval aviation are going to be in the direction of heavier and larger planes. I think that the Department of National Defence must see the necessity of having facilities for a purely military or naval airport in the Halifax area which will be immediately able to accommodate exclusively military traffic of all types in the event of an emergency.
The fact is that the facilities of the Dartmouth air base are apparently not suitable now to carry present military traffic of the heaviest type, and, unless considerably improved, certainly will not be in a position to take care of the military traffic which it may be required to handle in an emergency within even a very few years. From the civilian point of view the airport is not capable now of accommodating civilian traffic of a heavy type, and in this field development is also bound to be towards the use of larger, heavier and more economical planes. I would submit to the minister that the Department of National Defence, from a purely military point of view, in the near future will have to make some provision in the immediate Halifax area for the accommodation of much heavier aircraft than are being used by the fleet air arm at the Eastern Passage base. The other departments of government should, at the same time, consider the provision of facilities of a civilian nature for the accommodation of heavy aircraft traffic.
I am going to ask the minister to give us an assurance that the request will be considered, which I have already made to him in correspondence, that the officers of his department consult with the officers of the Department of Transport, and if necessary the officers of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and investigate carefully the immediate and future requirements for airport facilities in the Halifax area. If these

requirements, both military and civilian, can be met by an extension or improvement of the facilities of the airport at Eastern Passage, and if such extension can be carried out and the airport's use for civilian traffic continued without unreasonably restricting the use of the airport for necessary military and naval purposes, then we request that his officers co-operate with the officers of the other departments concerned in carrying out such improvement and extension. If after careful consideration by all the departments concerned it is not felt that the extension or improvement of this airport at Eastern Passage could be carried out to conveniently provide the facilities that are required, then we ask the officers of his department to give any assistance which may be necessary to the other departments of government in providing additional facilities elsewhere.
The minister is aware that he and other ministers concerned have received a copy of a resolution adopted by the Halifax city council on May 26 last. This resolution, and other communications which have been received by the minister, indicate the importance of this question and the interest which is naturally being taken in it in the Halifax area. I hope the minister will be able to give me the assurance that I ask, and that the consultations which I have suggested to him in correspondence as well as on the floor of the house will take place with the greatest possible speed, so that the unsatisfactory situation which now exists will be dealt with adequately.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hon. members in discussing these estimates have made a number of comments, and put forward a number of suggestions, and asked a number of questions which should be dealt with at this time. The nature of these would require considerable time to deal with in detail, because a good many of them involve questions of opinion concerning an appreciation of the present situation from a defence point of view, about which there are conflicting views. I should like to try to answer some of the points as briefly as possible.
In the first place, with regard to the effect of the announcement made following the London meeting of the council of the North Atlantic treaty, I think hon. members should read with care the statement made in the house by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on June 5 of this year, which appears at page 3189 of Hansard. He was careful to indicate, in that part of the
Supply-National Defence statement dealing with defence, what the effect of it would be in so far as we could see. He said:
As far as this government is concerned, in our defence policy we have already accepted this principle and have been trying to relate our policy to the defence of an area rather than merely to the defence of a country. We have been going on that principle and we will gladly do what we can to continue its application.
Now that follows from the nature of the problem of Canadian defence, because our defence has never been envisaged as the defence of Canada alone but the defence of Canada as part of a continent, and indeed the defence of Canada as part of the defence of the western countries which would all be involved in the event of a war for our freedom. It is not envisaged that this principle of balanced forces, forces that will be balanced internationally, will have any immediate effect on our own defence planning or on our own defence program. It must be evident that the only immediate effect of great consequence would be in the case where the north Atlantic powers had a surplus of weapons or of personnel of any particular type. If they have a surplus over all, obviously it would be unwise for any country to begin to construct new equipment that would duplicate existing equipment which is considered adequate.
For example, and I only mention it as an example because this has not received consideration yet, take the case of battleships or cruisers. It is quite possible that the view of those responsible for north Atlantic planning may be that we have enough battleships and enough cruisers. If so it would not be in the interests of total defence of the area to go ahead with the construction of more battleships and more cruisers. That is of course an extreme example, but it is an example of the way in which this will work.
We regard this principle as of great importance, indeed it is implicit in the idea of collective defence principle. It makes sense. But we do not believe it will have any immediate or very considerable effect on our own defence forces, because our defence planning has envisaged the operation of our defences in conjunction with other nations at all times. While I assure hon. members who asked questions on this point that it is not expected it will have any immediate effect on our defence program, I add that we will be ready to sit down with the representatives of the other nations and consider what should be done to attain the best possible results. We will enter those discussions, as we have in the past, with a free mind and with a strong desire to secure the best possible result.

Supply-National Defence
Perhaps I might supplement this by another statement on the question of commitments. The position is just as I have stated it in the house time after time, that is that the undertakings we have made in the North Atlantic treaty, particularly those contained in articles 3 and 5, are of a political character. When my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to those as "commitments", I think the expression "commitment" is equivalent to the expression "undertaking". But when I was asked if we had any commitments, I was considering this question from the point of view of specific military commitments; and I told the house then, as I tell the committee now, that we have not. I am not too sure that the North Atlantic treaty organization will ever develop in a way in which there are specific military commitments. That remains to be seen. It remains to be worked out. But if there are to be specific military commitments, those commitments will be the ones which are agreed to by the government of Canada made known to the parliament of Canada. That is expressly provided for in the terms of the treaty itself.

It is article 11, which refers to constitutional authorities of each country.
With regard to the development of this principle, as I say it is implicit in the very nature of collective defence and the concept of collective defence from the start. It grew out of our own meetings of the defence committee on April 1. A most significant statement on the subject was made by General Bradley in an address given before the executives club of Chicago on April 14, 1950, in which he definitely anticipated the nature of the decision with regard to balanced forces. I will not delay the committee by reading it, but it is an important statement indeed and one which I am sure will carry with it the judgment of all hon. members.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: Where is it found? Where is it available?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
It appeared in the New York Times for the following day.
With regard to another allied subject which was raised by the hon. member for Kamloops, as to whether our emphasis on the acquisition of equipment has changed, I can assure him that any change there has been in that respect was envisaged at the time when I made the statement I made in the house on June 24,


1948, when I referred to some dangers in defence planning. I said that one danger is that the Soviet union, without any genuine change of attitude, may suddenly appear to be seeking co-operation which might result in a slackening of effort.
And I said that:
A second danger is that we should come to regard war as inevitable.
And also I said:
A third danger is that we should commit our future resources to expenditures, equipment and plans that will be out of date when needed.
In that statement I do not think any hon. member can find anything to cavil at for an instant. That was the only basis, as far as I know, for that "wait and see" editorial of the Montreal Gazette of March 17, 1948. I must say that that editorial and similar statements are typical examples of first distorting what I said and then criticizing me for the distortion. I think our attitude on this matter has been perfectly plain.
May I give an example. We have a large number of anti-aircraft guns in Canada. They are of the most modern type at the end of the last world war. They are still good guns. They could be modified with the addition of types of equipment at a cost of about $180,000 a gun. The question is:	Is that type of gun
going to be useful five years from now, and should we incur the expenditure of $180,000 a gun in respect of this particular weapon? That is a question of judgment on which we have got to take the advice of the experts in this and other countries. If we had at our disposal unlimited sums of money, then of course we should make the modernization just as soon as we could. But since our money is not unlimited by any manner of means, we have got to do the best we can with it. If now we believe that at the end of five years we may anticipate another means of effectively dealing with aircraft, then we have got to balance the pros and the cons and make the best decision we can.
Then with regard to the provision of aircraft and antisubmarine vessels, may I say that we did not proceed with the production of the CF-100 in 1948 and 1949 because the CF-100 had not yet been developed. We knew that it was in course of development. We had been working on it already for two years and we hoped that it would be a successful aircraft. As soon as it began to seem likely that it would be a successful aircraft, we placed an order for tooling, and a preproduction order; and we are now negotiating an order for a larger number of aircraft.
The same thing is true with regard to the F-86. We did not order the F-86 or start production on it because there were not

F-86's in 1947. But as soon as that aircraft had been tested and proved to be successful, we made the decision to go ahead with the production of 100 of them at Canadair Limited.
With regard to the statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo about this particular aircraft, I must say that the figures he gave as to its performance, when the matter came up in the house before, are not in accordance with the information we have. This is not an obsolete aircraft. I was in the United States not long ago and went with the President of the United States and the Secretary of Defence, the Hon. Louis Johnson, and saw a great demonstration of the air power of the United States at Eglin field in Florida. It is the air proving ground. There we were given a book of photographs of the different types of aircraft. Here we have one of the photographs with the caption:
The air force's B-36, giant intercontinental bomber, beating off an interception attempt by the crack F-86 Sabre.
Then over the page:
The North American F-86 "Sabre," first line operational fighter of USAF tactical fighter groups is paced by the North American B-45 "Tornado," jet fight bomber. The "Sabre," fully armed, holds the world's speed record of 670 plus.
This aircraft is the fastest aircraft in production known to us anywhere in the world. Far from being obsolete, it is the 'first-line aircraft in the United States. The rate of climb given by the hon. member for Nanaimo, when the matter came up before, was quite different from the actual rate of climb. Information about this is restricted in the United States, but I saw this aircraft and three others climb in a demonstration; and I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that this one overtook the others as if they were virtually standing still.

speechtext:
They were the second and third fighter jets in the United States at the present time. With regard to the choice of the F-86 vis-a-vis the Vampire, I have already given the reasons for that in the house. We wanted to have an aircraft made in Canada that could be made according to North American specifications and produced in the event of an emergency here. It seemed to us to make sense that the capacity of the British plants to produce aircraft should be used in Britain and in the other countries
Supply-National Defence in Europe under the North Atlantic treaty. Further, the Vampire to which the hon. member for Nanaimo has referred, if there is one having anything like the specifications he mentions, is still not beyond the development stage. There is not even a prototype yet. We will have the F-86 in production in Canada according to North American standards and specifications before we could possibly obtain the Vampire to which the hon. member made reference.
The hon. member for Calgary East asked me a number of questions with which I should deal. He asked about the two fighter squadrons and whether they were up to strength. Yes, they are up to strength in personnel, and they are up to peacetime strength in respect of aircraft. Then he asked whether the brigade group was up to strength. I can tell him that it is at 80 per cent of the establishment. I might say, since the hon. member has expressed interest in it before, that at the present time we have more trained paratroopers in Canada than landed in the low countries in the German invasion in May, 1940.
Then the hon. member asked if the radar equipment we had was adequate and if the interceptor plans were adequate. I have already dealt with this question at some length in the house before, and pointed out that if we were to endeavour to have an air interception system on anything like the scale they had in England during the second world war we would be putting not only $425 million into defence, but a great deal more, and we would not be doing anything else.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Just so there will be no
misunderstanding, I did not ask whether the radar net and so forth were adequate for our defence. As a matter of fact I specifically said that they were not. I admitted it was impossible to produce in this country a defence which was really adequate to the country; that all we could hope to achieve was what you might call a minimum necessity. What I asked was whether the minister's own statement of what was to be provided in the way of a radar net, fighter squadrons and so forth, had been met.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am very much obliged to the hon. member. I misunderstood him. We are making progress on it. We have a plan under which we will do a certain amount of construction of radar sites and equipment each year. We have on order, in the way of equipment of the latest and most powerful sets, equipment to the value of approximately

Supply-National Defence $25 million. We also have a considerable quantity of mobile equipment, which can be used in any locality at any time.
We are moving ahead with the organization of reserve air force radar units. There is a very successful one in Montreal, as the first, with a strength today of some 500. That is being spread throughout the province of Quebec, -with sub-units in Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Sherbrooke, Three Rivers and Quebec city. That will be followed by the establishment of similar units in Toronto, Vancouver, and in other places. We have acquired the building necessary for the unit at Vancouver, and the organization, of the unit will be proceeded with at a very early date.

It is a building formerly used as a club in the centre of the city.
The hon. member for Three Rivers asked about the justification for the Magnificent. He was rather opposed by his colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops, which just indicates-

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: No, he was not opposed.

speechtext: I think the record will show that whereas the hon. member for Three Rivers questioned the desirability of having one aircraft carrier on the east coast, the hon. member for Kamloops endeavoured to make an argument in favour of having one on the west coast as well.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: The record will not show that.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am sorry if I misunderstood the hon. member.
To answer the hon. member for Three Rivers, the justification for an aircraft carrier in a country like Canada of course is that an aircraft carrier is considered to be an essential weapon today for antisubmarine activities. Whether or not that will be so five or ten years from now remains to be seen, depending on the development of other types of equipment. At the present time I should think that certainly it is the view of everyone that aircraft carriers are necessary for use in connection with antisubmarine work. If that statement is accepted, as I think it should be, the question is, can we rely on having the use of an aircraft carrier from the United Kingdom or the United States on loan in order to enable us to do the training on our antisubmarine vessels. Our view is that since we had this aircraft carrier-it is the property of Britain-since we had a naval air arm established at the end of the last war, we would not be justified in making any radical change in the immediate future, but should carry on
[M*. Claxton.]
with the one aircraft carrier, watch the development of the art, keep up with it, and then if any alternative method of dealing with it, or if this concept of planned forces developed to a very great degree, then we might reconsider the position; but certainly so far as we can see ahead we mean to maintain the aircraft carrier.
With regard to the expenditures on it, the answer to the question put in the house related to the cost of operation of the aircraft carrier only. I think the hon. member mentioned the figure of $4,500,000. My recollection is that that is substantially the answer given. Then he referred to a statement credited to the chief of the naval services in Vancouver that it was costing $20 million. The chief of the naval services has told me that he did not make any such statement. The actual figure for the over-all cost of the operation of the aircraft carrier, including the maintenance of the base at Dartmouth and everything that should properly be included, is approximately $10 million a year.
We could, as has been suggested, operate a destroyer at a cost of $2 million or $2,500,000 a year, but it would not provide nearly the same training facilities for active and reserve personnel; and of course it would mean that we would not have the services of an aircraft carrier for training in antisubmarine work.

speechtext: As I said, the chief of naval staff told me that he did not say that.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: Both papers are wrong, then?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, or. else the chief of naval staff is wrong in his recollection. However, he told me that he did not give the figure of $20 million.
The hon. member for Calgary East asked for an explanation of the amounts I had given with respect to expenditures on the air force. The table which appeared in Hansard gives a figure of 40-6 per cent whereas in a statement later I mentioned a figure, he said, of 44-8 per cent. The reason for that is that in the second figure I was giving the proportion of the defence dollar spent for the navy, army and air force. That gives the result the hon. member mentioned. However, if you include pensions, grants, defence research and the like, and take them separately, as is done in this table, the result is 40-6 per cent. Pensions, grants, research and so on are applicable over the services roughly in proportion to the other expenditures.
The hon. member then asked as to the state of training in the reserve forces, and what the target was. The target is to have the reserve forces trained up to the standard of the active forces. That is being achieved with officers, N.C.O.'s and tradesmen. However, it takes considerable time, on the basis of present training, to bring the rank and file up to those standards. It is hoped that those standards would be achieved over a period of approximately three years.
As to the state of equipment: the reserve forces have more equipment than they have ever had before. There is adequate equipment of mo'dern types for all units-in fact, most units have more equipment than they have storage space in which to accommodate it.
I was asked about the state of recruiting. The hon. member for Calgary East referred to a statement I had made that recruiting did not need help. What was intended was acceleration. At that time the rate of recruiting in the active force-and I specified the active force-was quite satisfactory. It has been moving along in a satisfactory way for the last
Supply-National Defence three years. Recruiting for the reserve force has been good in recent months. We would like to see it continued and better. We have in the active force 47,000 and in the reserve force 49,000, so that it is increasing steadily. However, we would like to have another 4,000, or 5,000 just as soon as we can get them in the reserve force. I think that in proportion to population Canada has more men in the reserve force than has any other country in the commonwealth. As I have indicated time and again to hon. members, and also to others, we are exceedingly glad to get every possible help we can in recruiting. I have made appeals to that effect to hon. members, to branches of the Legion and to others.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South referred to educational standards for the armed forces. We are in the position that at the present time we are getting men, at about the rate we want them, who have the very high standards we think we ought to get. If we accept men with lower standards we will have to give them in-service education, which will cost both personnel and money, and postpone their incorporation into the units in which they are to serve. It seems to us we should not seek to diminish the standards, but that we should endeavour to raise them as high as we can.
The hon. member for Calgary East expressed satisfaction with the procedure of having officers from North Atlantic treaty countries trained at our expense in the army and air force of Canada. I was glad to hear him say that. He said that the figures were small-only one hundred for the air force and one hundred and fifty for the army.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I said "comparatively
small".

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: Yes, comparatively small. Well, in comparison with the numbers actually being trained, particularly in the air services in other countries at the present time, those are quite satisfactory figures. He also asked how many men we had training abroad. We have as staff and students in service and training abroad 405 officers and men of the three services.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: How is that split up?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
What countries are those for?

Supply-National Defence

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: The United States, England and a number of other countries. These include officers and men serving abroad as well as training abroad, because if they are serving abroad they are usually developing useful experience as well as training.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: Does that include air attaches?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Yes, there are seven or eight air, naval and military attaches. The hon. member for Calgary East asked about civil defence plans. I have already made a statement to the effect that we have completed a plan of organization at the federal level. I should explain that when General Worthington was appointed co-ordinator of civil defence we had him look into what has been done in the United Kingdom, the United States and other countries. Then he went about to discuss the matter with the provinces. Following that we worked out a basis for a plan with all the government departments concerned. At the request of the provinces General Worth-, ington put before them the results of that work. That part of the operation has just been completed but late in the summer or early in the autumn we propose to get together the representatives of the provinces in order to carry forward the organization at the provincial level. As we envisage civil defence we consider it largely a matter for co-operation of the closest kind with the provinces, and through them with the municipalities.
The hon. member for Cape Bteton South and the hon. member for Halifax referred to the airport at Dartmouth which at present is operated as a land base for the fleet air arm. The airport is quite adequate for that purpose but if aircraft heavier than 60,000 pounds are to land the runway strips would be damaged and major damage would be caused. There is an item in the estimates this year for the maintenance of the runways and we will endeavour to keep them in condition in order to maintain the existing use.
With regard to developing the airport or increasing its size and capacity, I shall be glad to discuss again with the representatives of the Department of Transport the possible desirability of increasing the capacity of the airport along the lines suggested by the senior member for Halifax, both today and in correspondence, and also by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
The defence of the Pacific was raised by the hon. member for Kamloops. I think it is axiomatic that a country like Canada can be defended only as part of the continent. It is obvious that we are in the fortunate position of being well to the east of lines of defence which include Japan and the islands to the south and the Hawaiian islands, and Alaska in the north. We are not in the same


exposed position in the Pacific as we are in the Atlantic. However, the approximate size of the fleets and their distribution are much the same. The concept of coastal defence by static means seems to be passing out. It is much more likely that goastal defence will be secured by the operation of aircraft that are largely shore-based, and by the use of amphibian aircraft. On that account we are keeping our hands on the base at Patricia Bay and the other airfields, and are maintaining the air force establishment at Vancouver.
The hon. member for Calgary East asked about the progress made in standardization. We have made great progress in the standardization of procedure and battle orders and the like with the United States and also with the United Kingdom and other countries of the western union. There is now a generally accepted system of communications and battle procedure which would enable the forces of the countries of the North Atlantic pact to operate together. As a matter of fact, as hon. members know, great progress was made in this respect by the end of the second world war and that progress has been continued since. We can operate, certainly without any difficulty, with the forces of either the United Kingdom or the United States. Exercise Sweetbriar showed clearly that the staffs and the communications systems and everything necessary to operate armed forces, even under the difficult conditions of the sub-Arctic, could work together very well. I think I have covered most of the points raised by hon. members. If not, I am sure they will bring them to my attention.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: There was one matter in connection with Pacific defence I should like to have cleared up. I did not say that we should have an aircraft carrier on the west coast. I was simply asking whether I was right in assuming that aircraft carriers were an integral part of the antisubmarine task force. I then went on to ask what would be done to bring the Pacific antisubmarine defence up to at least a par with the Atlantic. The minister indicated that they are part of such a task force and answered my question in part, but I should like him to deal with the matter of naval units on the Pacific coast.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: If we had more money to spend on defence and if we did not have to do other things that have greater priority I would like to have an aircraft carrier on the west coast as well, but, as has been indicated, that would cost $10 million a year and our view is that one is better than none.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Is not a great part of your cost in maintaining shore establishments and

headquarters and could not a second carrier be maintained without duplicating entirely that expense?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Our experience is that because of the geography of Canada there is a necessity to have the forces divided between the Pacific and the Atlantic. The overhead and operation in each case is separate and distinct. You must duplicate virtually every service. If Canada was fortunate in having only one major naval establishment we could reduce that overhead substantially, but as it is now we have to duplicate the dockyard machinery, equipment, personnel, stores, magazines and everything else on each coast. There is a considerable amount of duplication which is inevitable because of the geography of the country.
I shall look over my notes and if there is anything further I can deal with it at eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
