speechtext:
Order. It is a matter to be dealt with when the Speaker is in the chair and not in committee.
Supply-National Defence

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: Well, get the Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: Shall item 202 carry?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I told the hon. member for
Calgary East that I would check my notes and answer all the points that he and other members of the opposition raised. In addition to the other points the hon. member mentioned before, he referred to the position of western Germany and Spain. Surely that is a matter for external affairs and one of general foreign policy. I can assure him that the status of western Germany and Spain are matters of great concern to the North Atlantic treaty nations and as he indicated himself they are thorny questions. I do not think he would wish me to express any view on them at this time.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: What I said was that if the defence chiefs of our services had expressed any views on these matters I thought the committee should have the advantage of them.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
These are matters which concern not only ourselves but France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, the United Kingdom, Denmark, and all the other nations under the North Atlantic treaty. It would not be proper for me to express any views to the committee at this time with regard to the question raised by the hon. member. I do not think that would help the situation, which is one that has to be worked out over quite a long term in conjunction with our allies. As the hon. member indicated, they are "thorny" questions, and I am not in a position to make any further comment.
In the same passage of his remarks the hon. member referred to a new strategy to the effect that we should not simply attempt the liberation of the countries of western Europe after they have been overrun. I can assure him that there is nothing new in that. That has been the view of the countries of the western union since it was formed, of Benelux and of the North Atlantic treaty nations ever since their inception. There would not be very much point in the alliance of the countries of western Europe if it simply provided that after they were overrun by an aggressor they would subsequently be liberated by other countries.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: This is the first time it has been definitely stated.	.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I do not know whether or not it was stated before in the communiques issued by the North Atlantic treaty powers, but certainly it has been implicit in the North

Supply-National Defence Atlantic treaty organization from start to finish that we would endeavour to organize and perfect a system of defence so that we can defend our freedom and that of the other countries with which we are associated in the best place to defend it, wherever that may be.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Would the minister permit a question on that point? I should like to refer to an article written for the London Observer and printed in the Globe and Mail of June 2. It is apropos of what is being discussed. The article reads in part:
It is impossible to overrate its importance.
The reference is to the importance of the decision made.
It commits America, Canada and Britain, no longer only to the rescue of Europe but to the defence of Europe.
I do not suppose it was ever consciously said that previously it was only for the rescue of Europe, but is it not correct, as has been repeatedly stated since the London decision, that this decision now brings it much nearer the realm of practical policy?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I think it may be so that this is a decision on a question of principle which will help to assist the north Atlantic powers to achieve what was their object before. Nevertheless it was always their abject to defend each other. That is stated in the treaty, and one of the undertakings therein is to come to each other's defence if any one is attacked.
Then the hon. member for Calgary East asked what has been done with regard to the provision of tracked vehicles. I can tell him that work with regard to the development of tracked vehicles of a suitable type is being carried on in Canada at the Ford Motor Company and at Churchill. We are continuing to work on our own types of tracked vehicles, but we also hope that in consequence of the experiences of the exercise we will develop even better tracked vehicles in co-operation with the United States.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: May I ask if any increase has been made in the number of tracked vehicles provided to the active units of the permanent force?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
Not yet, no. We have tracked vehicles of the type I mentioned in my previous remarks on this subject available for issue if we should have an exercise of this type or .the opportunity to use them again.
The hon. member said that the disasters in Winnipeg and other places showed the need of civilian organization. I believe that is a matter for the provinces and municipalities

across Canada. But I can assure him that at no stage of the operations, either in Winnipeg, the Fraser valley, Rimouski or Cabano, was there any indication that there was any failure on the part of the federal government agencies, including the armed forces, to co-operate with the civilian authorities. We propose, in consequence of these experiences, to develop further the doctrine of aid to the civil power in the event of emergencies, which has I think admittedly worked so well in these cases, and also extend to the provinces and municipalities the result of our experience with regard to disasters of a civil character not related to an emergency of the nature of war. What we aim to do is co-operate with them, and work with them in every way possible.
Then the hon. member asked about progress with regard to United States-Canadian procurement. A statement was made about that in the house.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: I said that.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: Yes. It represents a very great step forward. In consequence of the announcement made in Washington that authority had been given to permit the procurement of $15 million to $25 million of defence equipment in Canada, we are endeavouring to negotiate with representatives of the United States to see how the matter can best be dealt with, and what items can best be made available.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: What I asked was, in a general way, what sort of equipment, material and so forth would be produced by Canada and sold to the United States; and what, in a general way, would be the type of thing the United States would produce and sell to us.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: That is one of the questions that have to be explored. There is hardly any type of equipment that Canada could make which has not already been produced by the. United States.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: That is one of the reasons I asked the question.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
On the other hand, there are many types of equipment which we could produce in Canada just as economically as they could be produced in the United States, provided we got an economic run to permit us to arrive at the lowest possible price. What those items will be depends on negotiations. We could, for example, produce any type of guns up to possibly the 105 in Canada just as economically as they will be produced in the United States, if those guns were required in large numbers. On the other hand, it might possibly be more economic for us to acquire heavier equipment, heavier motor vehicles,

from the United States. Our general aim is to achieve a rough kind of balance with regard to defence procurements from both countries. At the present time we have under purchase from the United States components of the F-86 totalling $11 million, plus a great deal of other equipment. We would like to see that figure balanced by similar United States purchases of equipment from Canada, but that is a matter of negotiation. The announcement made last week in the United States resulted from a considerable period of negotiation.
The hon. member referred to the total amount we were asked to vote, and said we were committing parliament to $625 million. The actual amount sought by these estimates is, of course, $425 million. No other cash appropriation is sought under these votes, but we do ask an additional current commitment authority for accounting purposes of $54,245,696, and then future commitment authority in respect of future years amounting to $144,181,470. That is in order to permit us, with some authority from parliament, to make long-term contracts for the production of aircraft, shipbuilding, electronic equipment and so on, which cannot be produced within the current fiscal year. That applies to a great range of defence equipment, even cloth and uniforms for the armed forces. The actual amount sought is $425 million.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: To clarify that, does it mean that, including the vote for the research branch, we are being asked to make commitments for this year or future years of an extra $200 million, approximately?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: No, sir; the money that must be found for any commitment must be found out of each year's appropriation. On the other hand contractors would like to have some authority at least back of the contracts which we make with them extending beyond the current fiscal year; that is the effect of the future year's commitment authority. It enables us, for example, in the case of aircraft to undertake a program extending over a period of several years; but in respect of the payment to be made for each year, we must of course obtain appropriations from parliament.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I had quite a long discussion with the minister last year over the appropriateness of having the future commitments included. I shall not go into that again at the moment. Nevertheless, I think he will agree that the general effect of these commitments, which he says are to enable him to place contracts more readily, is to make it appear that the present session of parliament has entered into commitments for approximately $200 million.
Supply-National Defence

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: That is always subject to the money being voted by parliament year by year. The appropriation for this year is $425 million.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: Then, what is the real need for them? Would any contractor refuse to fake a contract if you were not able to point out to him that you had this authority, as you say, for what it is worth? It is not worth much, if you can imagine an appropriation not being voted. When I first heard of these future commitments, I was rather impressed by them. The more I think of them, the less I am impressed by them as either proper or appropriate.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: With regard to the propriety, I can assure the hon. gentleman I did not introduce this practice. It was done in order that we might plan defence in a sensible way over a period of years, and so that the officials of the treasury department and finance department could see what would be involved in future years' commitments in respect of contracts undertaken this year. It strikes me that is a desirable thing to do. It does not obligate parliament later to vote the money, but it does indicate to the contractor that parliament is likely to vote the money. I have never heard of parliament refusing to vote money for such a purpose before.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: That is what I was going to say. It seems to me it works against this.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: It seems to me it does put on the department the responsibility for planning its future commitments over a period of years. For example, in respect of the sum of $144,181,470, about $50 million odd is applicable to the year 1951-52; $41 million to the year 1952-53; $27 million to the year 1953-54; and $24 million to the year 1954-55. It therefore provides for an orderly way of defence planning in order to achieve treasury control.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
If I might just comment on that matter for a moment, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that a commitment of this sort either binds or it does not bind. If it does not bind, it is of no value whatever. If it does bind, it means that we are in effect voting a further $200 million, approximately. The minister evidently thinks that it has some value. If it has any value, it must have some value to bind us to make these commitments. In that event I think we have got to get back to the original point that I brought out and mentioned when I spoke this morning and immediately after the noon adjournment: that is that we are in effect this year voting about $625 million,

Supply-National Defence $425 million of which is to be spent immediately and the other $200 million of which we are to some extent, at any rate, bound to expend.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
In order to comply with the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, before we can have a contract we must have a commitment authority. In order that we may have a contract extending beyond the current fiscal year, we must have a commitment authority extending beyond the current fiscal year. The alternative to doing it this way,
I suggest, would be to make a contract, let us say, for ten aircraft in respect of 1950-51. We would then arrive at a price per aircraft that would be fantastic. Then towards the end of that year, as we got authority from parliament, through the appropriation, we would make a contract for another 50 aircraft to be produced in 1951-52, and so on. The proposal practice permits us to conform with the terms of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act and to make a forward commitment which will enable us to secure the advantage of a continuous run so as to secure an economic price. I understand this is also done in the Department of Public Works which is about the only other department having a similar problem.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: I am not arguing with the minister as to whether the practice is valuable or whether it is not. On the basis of his explanation, it would appear that it was a valuable practice. Without studying it further, I cannot subscribe to it. Nevertheless, as I say, it would appear that that is the case. The basic point I think is this. Whether it is good practice or whether it is not, the practical effect of it is that we are in effect committing ourselves to expenditures of $625 million rather than $425 million by this action.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman must be fair. In respect of the year 1950-51, the only commitment and the only money available for expenditure by the Department of National Defence is $425 million. In arriving at the size of the estimates for next year, as was done in the case of the estimates this year, we had to take account of our forward commitments that had been made previously as authorized by parliament. Parliament has full control over the cash; but it makes sense for us to be able to make a contract in respect of deliveries and possible payments beyond the current fiscal year. I suggest that is fundamental to defence procurement.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext:
I quite appreciate what the minister has said and I agree that the actual amount which it is estimated will be spent this year will be $425 million. There was


just one point that I do not think was quite correct. The minister said that is all that they can possibly spend. In item 202 this language is used: "to make commitments for the current year of $438,178,000", not $384 million as appears in the column on the right-hand side, and "commitments for future years of $141,123,670". As I read the thing, the department, if it wanted to, could spend not $384 million under this item but $438 million.

speechtext: No, sir. I am sorry, but the hon. gentleman is not right. All we can spend is the money voted by parliament; which is, $425 million. But in order to facilitate the work of the department and also to comply with the provisions of section 29 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, we can make from moment to moment commitments up to an additional sum of $54,245,696.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF A RESIDENCE FOR THE PRIME MINISTER OF CANADA
speechtext: That is for this year. We can make commitments but we cannot spend anything more than $425 million. The reason for that is to permit us to deal with this kind of situation. In the preparation of the estimates of a department like Defence, every unit commander must provide let us say, for the fuel of his unit: coal, gasoline and so on. He puts in an item which will be, he estimates, sufficient to take care of anything that may be required. There is no extra factor included. There is nothing for contingencies. He puts down, however, a figure which he is reasonably certain will take care of the requirements of his unit for that year. If all the units put in figures on that basis, the average experience of the units will be less than the expectancy. If we did not have this additional commitment authority, around about the month of January or February we would not be able to make commitments against unencumbered funds in respect even of salaries, wages, pay and allowances, and food because of the necessity for each person ensuring that he has enough to get by with until the year is ended, irrespective of the actual experience that year. By this means, therefore, I think we can secure the greatest possible safety and also the greatest possible economy under the control of parliament over the total sum appropriated. Otherwise we would have a larger estimate to do the same work and an extremely large unexpended balance at the end of each year because of the nature of the defence operations.

I have not been arguing here, Mr. Chairman, against the necessity of these things. I say they may be quite necessary. But as I understand the minister's explanation of this last point about this $54 million, the actual fact is that under this item

the department is able to incur debts of $54 million during the current year. In other words, they can run up bills, just the same as you and I might do at the grocery store. If we did not have enough money to pay our bill this month, we would have it run; and if we were still short of money next month, we would have it run during that month, and we would always be assuring the grocer that, come March 31, we would get the money and be able to pay him the amount of the bill. It seems to me that that is the position this $54 million is in. Under this item the department is given authority to run up a bill of $54 million which, of course, will be paid when we vote the estimates for the next year, 1951-52. Therefore the total effect is that in addition to voting this $384 million we are making a commitment to pay a further $54 million.

I do not consider myself
qualified to make comments or criticize the technical application, distribution or use of defence funds. It is sufficient for me to say
Supply-National Defence that I have every confidence in the minister in the administration of his department; but I do rise, Mr. Chairman, because I was particularly interested in some remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar. I wish to draw to the minister's attention a case similar to the one he mentioned. While I may not be an expert on military matters, I think I am quite competent to raise my voice as a member of this house to defend the civil liberties of the soldier and the civilian.
On my return home from the last session of parliament I was told by several people in my constituency that there had been a visit from someone in the army to a certain district with respect to a man who had long service in the forces. The general gossip in the village was that he was going to be discharged because he was a member of or sympathetic to the Labour-Progressive party, or something of that sort. I understand that later this man was discharged, and his discharge certificate read:	"Not likely to become an efficient
soldier". Later, on protests being made, that certificate was altered so that there was no objection to the terms of the discharge. I want to bring to the minister's attention the facts of this case. This man served four years in the first world war; he served five years in the second world war; he served five years in the permanent forces after the second world war. Then his department discharged him as not likely to become an efficient soldier. I think that was most unfair to that man in view of the fact that unfortunate gossip was general around the village and it was completely unfounded.
If an official of the minister's department goes to a small village and visits the butcher, the baker and the gas station operator and tells them why he is there it takes only twenty-four hours for everyone in that district to know what he was there for. I rise on behalf of that man, who served his country well. Fortunately the mistake has been corrected, though of course there are still some people who think the former gossip had some foundation.
As a matter of fact, this man is altogether unpolitically minded. I do not think he would realize the essential difference between the policy of the Progressive Conservative party and the policy of the C.C.F. I wish he would. I have talked to him on several occasions without any effect. He is one of those members of the working class who still have a great deal of faith in Toryism.
I wish to bring this matter to the attention of the minister because I think great care must be taken to prevent that sort of thing being done by an indiscreet official who visits

Supply-National Defence a small village or community. I do hope that the greatest care will be taken in a case like this and in cases such as those mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, where there are supposed grounds for suspicion. I realize the necessity for security and support every care being taken to protect our defence arrangements, but I do ask again that great care be taken in a case like this, particularly in small places, because these things are not easily forgotten, and in this case a grave injustice was done to a very decent chap indeed.
Before sitting down I want to mention to the minister that several representative groups in my riding and responsible individuals have suggested to me that I bring to the minister's attention the fact that they are particularly interested in some permanent plans for civil defence. It has been mentioned to me that even if a skeleton organization were established so that these men could be getting some training they could be used in such emergencies as flood disasters and fighting forest fires. Even if there were a skeleton group of some organization they would gain experience in training and all the rest of it, and they could be used in the local district to support the forest branch in the event of forest fires, and other emergencies.
I should also like to return to the matter with which I dealt yesterday, namely, the question of chaplains in the defence forces having commissions. The minister explained the situation very well, and I am quite satisfied with his explanation to me at that time; but I want to repeat that I have met a large number of men of the three forces, and a good many members of the major religious denominations in this country, and some of the clergy of all the major denominations, who have expressed to me the opinion that it is not in the best interests of the men in the armed forces, and not in the best interests of the church, for the chaplains to have commissioned rank.
I should like the minister to advise the committee what are the pay allowances and what cars are provided for the chaplains of the honorary ranks of colonel, major and captain.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few observations of a general nature. I am not going into any involved discussion on training or equipment. I got a lesson in that in the autumn of 1939, when the second war broke out, which I think will do me for the rest of my life. I was asked to go to a meeting of members of my old battery, and I found that they were terribly anxious to be allowed to do some training with the new units.
As I listened to them for a little while I began to laugh. They said, "What are you laughing at?" I said, "I am trying to imagine what you would have felt like in 1915 if you were told you were going to be taught by veterans of the South African war." I never made such a successful argument in my life. They dropped it like a hot potato, because they realized that our war in 1914-18 was several years further removed from the second war than our war from the South African war.
However, I should like to say something about the general situation. We are engaged here in the voting of hundreds of millions of dollars for defence. To me it is an astonishing thing that there should be comparatively little interest throughout the country in this matter. I go further and say it is astonishing that in a democracy apparently in peacetime we cannot prepare for either peace or war.

After the first war I was one of those-and they were regarded as rather a queer lot-who tried to do something for the League of Nations Society. But you could not get people interested in peace. They were bored with it then. They would not do any work about it. I think it is reasonable to say, looking back, that if people had been more keen about it something might have been done.
Today the difficulty is greater, and I have no doubt whatever that those who are trying to do work for the United Nations are having the same trouble as we had twenty years ago -and probably more. On the other hand it is extremely difficult to get people to be interested in the question of defence, as we understand it. It is for that reason I am on my feet this evening. I should like to make a few observations because I think that that is where this government and parliament comes in.
The fact that we had a report made to us a few days ago by the Secretary of State for External Affairs raises the question as to whether we are not stepping into an entirely new phase in the matter of defence. I have one or two paragraphs I should like to read on the point. I wish to suggest that we think it is terribly important that the government somehow or other should let the people know about this. I do not know how they can do it, unless they let us know. If defence is going to be the private enterprise of the cabinet, and if the cabinet is not going to take the House of Commons into its confidence, then how much less will they be able to take the people into their confidence, and how much chance will the people have to realize the seriousness of the estimates which we are here about to discuss.
I should like to read briefly from an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of Friday, June 2, and, I have no doubt, in other newspapers. This is written by a responsible authority, although the author remains anonymous. It is headed "Defense of the West", and is written by "A Student of Europe". I take it that it is serious comment, because the article is a "special" to the London Observer and the Globe and Mail. First of all the writer says this:
Now the Atlantic treaty nations have "resolved by their united efforts, to build up a system of defense . . . capable of withstanding any external threat directed against any of them."
The article then states that there are two historic decisions, and he proceeds to set them out.
This is the first of the historic decisions taken by the Atlantic treaty council. It is impossible to overrate its importance. It commits America, Canada and Britain, no longer only to the rescue of Europe
Supply-National Defence but to the defense of Europe. It further commits them to build by "united efforts" with the western Europeans, a unified system of defense.
And one further thing I should like to read:
How will this Atlantic defense system have to be shaped to be effective? Some useful guidance can be had from a book which, by an odd coincidence, appeared on the very day of the Atlantic council's decision, Defense of the West, by Mr. Liddell Hart. He was writing long before that decision, and some parts of his book are outdated by it; but his main argument gains added pertinence.
Summarizing the rest of it he says, in effect, that it is not going to be numbers that count. He points out that a few German armoured divisions with 200,000 men overran the whole of Europe and defeated millions of opponents. He then goes on to make very definite suggestions as to changes in military preparation which are involved in the present situation.
The only reason for my bringing this up is that we have had differences of opinion as to how much information should be given to those of us in the opposition and, indeed, to private members on the government side. But I do suggest to the minister that if he desires, as I am sure he does desire, that the people throughout the country should take this matter seriously and understand the importance of it, then he has got to begin by taking it seriously in this House of Commons.
I should hope that he would bear in mind what has been said before to him, that it is quite impossible for members of parliament to make up their minds for themselves- and by that I mean, something more than just saying that the minister is a good fellow, and that everything is all right in his hands. It is easy enough to do that, but it does not enable us to know what is being done or to answer the questions we will be asked when we return to our constituencies.
There is another thing which the present method does not cover. I said to a newspaper friend of mine this afternoon, "Do you think there is any real interest in the matter of defence?" He said "People cannot be interested in millions". What he meant was people have to have something definite and practical in which to interest themselves.
I do suggest earnestly to the minister that, with this new situation before us, and with the new problems which have to be faced, the minister should consider-even reconsider-whether it is not possible that this House of Commons might be given much more information than it has been getting. I am not overlooking the question of security. No one but a fool wants things to be told that should not be told. But on the other hand no

Supply-National Defence one who is living in this world today can doubt that the great part of what we are doing is known to the Russians as well as it is to ourselves.
Of course we do talk much more frankly about these things than we did a few years ago. I think the minister should be more realistic in thinking about it and not merely back away from it, and give us what is inclined to be a service view. Years ago, during the first war when there was a question of information being given, a very responsible journalist commenting on this and on the withholding of information said, "We all know that there are many things which must not be told and we expect those things to be withheld. But, on the other hand, we can well imagine that there is a certain type of serviceman who says, 'What, the public wants to know? Well, damn them, they won't know' ". It is that kind of thing that we want to be protected against, both from the serviceman and, quite frankly, from our political associates.
I said I was going to be brief. I think I have covered all that I wanted to say. I take my seat saying this: We are being asked to spend-I will not haggle at the moment about a mere couple of hundred million; I will leave it at the lower figure-$425 million, which is quite a bunch of money. We in the opposition feel, and are entitled to feel, that unless we are taken into confidence more than we have been we cannot vote on this in an intelligent manner, by which I mean that we cannot make up our minds on direct evidence which is the only proper way for even semiintelligent people to make up their minds.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like very much to enable the hon. member for Greenwood to get the kind of information on which he can make up his mind; I should like to do that, but I just do not know how to do it. Day in and day out we have been subjected by the opposition to the charge of withholding information. Today some hon. members opposite said that we had held off presenting the estimates for the department of defence until the end of the session for some obscure purpose, which no doubt they were implying was a wrong one.
I want to tell this committee that I do not know of any information that has been withheld except that a year and a half ago when the hon. member for Calgary East asked for the strength of a parachute battalion which was trained and ready to face the enemy. I think that is the only specific question that I said I could not answer on security grounds, in addition to one or two others of a similar nature. On

the advice of my advisers I felt that it was not in the interests of our country to give to any prospective enemy the one bit of information he wanted. Apart from that, time has been spent unreasonably with the suggestion that we are withholding information, time that might have been better occupied in requesting information which I would have been glad to give.
With regard to the consideration of the estimates, may I say that in the years I have occupied this position, that is since the end of 1946, the discussion of the estimates of this department has not been curtailed by the lapse of time on any single occasion in any one of those years. It has ended when the questions that were put, which were not rhetorical questions but those seeking information, were answered and there were no more questions. I feel that this committee is entitled to get everything possible, and that has been my view right through. If there is anything that we can give that we have not given, tell us so that we can give it and not keep on saying that you have not information that you have never asked for.
Comparisons are frequently made, and properly so, between the practice in this house and that in Westminster. If hon. members will look at the debates of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom they will see that four days were set aside for the discussion of the defence estimates. They will see also that the discussion proceeded very much as it has this afternoon, with few inquiries for specific bits of information but a good deal of observation and suggestions, a good deal of puzzlement being indicated. That is all quite proper because these are puzzling and difficult times. But in the end the parliament at Westminster did not get anything like the quantity of information that is given to this parliament in respect to defence estimates. I do not try to justify our position because we have no position except to give everything that is reasonably possible. But I do say that when we are continually charged with refusing to give information when the information is not even asked for, then I think we ought to get on to the next question.
With regard to the observations of the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. -member for Calgary East and the hon. member for Kamloops, may I say that these are difficult times indeed. It is very difficult for us to know exactly what the next ten years will hold. We cannot report history until events have taken place. But the same difficulty occurs in every country. Our desire is to work together with those other countries in order that we may make the best possible use of the

resources put at our disposal by this parliament, speaking for the people of Canada, for the defence of our country, and not only of our country but of all countries with which we are allied.
I suggest that that is our object, and I am sure that that is the object of all members. I am sure that that is the desire of the people. Contrary to the views expressed by the hon. member for Greenwood I believe that the interest in defence has never been greater than it is today. I believe that the support for national defence throughout the country has never been greater than it is today. By reason of that support and by reason of that interest we are having very considerable success in the development of our reserve army as well as of our active forces. They are people of whom the Canadian people can well be proud.
I would be only too glad to deal with these questions in any way in which they can be dealt with properly according to our rules and in accordance with the decisions of this house, but I really must resent the continual suggestion that I am withholding information. If hon. members feel that I am doing that, then I assure them that it is for no other reason than that the uncertainties that are ahead cause one who is in a position of responsibility to be pretty cautious about his prophecies for the future.
If you look at the discussions in congress or in any of the other parliaments of the commonwealth you will see that there has been expressed exactly the same point of view as was expressed by the hon. member for Greenwood. I must say that I feel sympathy for his point of view, and I think he sympathizes with me in mine.

That was nothing, so I had two nothings. I am asking the question once more because the fishermen of Queens county are nervous about the matter. They are wondering whether they will have a bombing range in the neighbourhood of their best fishing territory off the north shore of Prince Edward Island. If it is outside the fourteen-mile limit I would not have much to say about it. I cannot see why they desire to have a bombing range there. Is it only because the R.C.A.F. unit want a range nearer to their base? There is a range off Chatham. It is marked as a danger zone, and it is only a few more miles for them to fly over there where they can conduct their bombing practice. I would like the minister to give a definite assurance to the fishermen of Queens county in Prince Edward Island as to where the bombing range is to be placed this coming summer.

We are working on that now. The hon. member for Kamloops raised a question of considerable interest and importance that I have not dealt with before, the matter of headstones on Canadian graves. I think it was first raised recently in an article in the Vancouver Sun and another article in the Victoria Times. It was raised first in the house by the hon. member for Nanaimo. Since then I have had it looked into, and it was found that in 1946, when arrangements for permanent headstones on Canadian graves were being made with the imperial war graves commission, instructions were given that resulted in infantry and armoured corps personnel being described in exactly the same way as members of the artillery, engineers, army service corps and other similar units, without reference to their


particular unit but with reference to their corps. The headstones would have the name, number, rank and the Canadian maple leaf. Then if they belonged to the Canadian infantry corps the headstones would have Canadian infantry corps on them in the same way as the artillery would be described as artillery. That was done before I took over this post. On the matter being raised again I have looked into it. I must say, having had a mixed service career in that I was in the artillery, like the leader of the opposition, and before that a member of an infantry unit, I can see both points of view. But I do think that the matter having been raised, and knowing the regimental traditions of the famous units of Canada, including the armoured corps-they are largely succeeding the cavalry-and the infantry, probably a considerable majority of the members of those units, and of their next of kin, would desire to see the names of the units put on the headstones. I found that a number of headstones have been erected with "Canadian Infantry Corps" or "Canadian Armoured Corps" on them, but pending further examination as to the possibility and desirability of what should be done I stopped further erection of headstones. We are actively exploring the possibility of having the names of the units of infantry and armoured corps put on the remaining headstones to be erected, and also replacing those already erected. At the present time that is certainly my own view, that it should be done; and that would be in accordance with the wishes of a great number of the men in the units and their dependents. That action has already been taken, and just as soon as we can secure a report on the situation from the imperial war graves commission, I shall make an announcement to the house. I hope it will be along the lines hon. members would like.

I should like to express immediately, on behalf of all the members, and those who have brought up the matter with the members, their gratification at the sympathetic attitude shown by the minister to that request. I hope the report receives the kind of consideration 'which will enable the steps to be taken which the minister has indicated he personally favours, namely, the placing of the individual units of infantry or armoured corps on the headstones of the graves overseas.
I should like to refer to the statement just made by the minister to the effect that he feels there is not much justification for the criticism that information has been denied. My attitude towards that question is not so much that we say the minister refuses to answer questions when asked during the course of the discussion on his estimates, as

that we are not in a position, owing to the manner in which the estimates are discussed in the committee of the whole, to direct the questions which will elicit the key information we desire. This matter has been discussed before, and I am not going into the details again, but so far as I am concerned that is the gist of the complaint. It is not that if we ask some general question we do not get a general answer. We do. But it is extremely difficult if not impossible under the procedure which we have in the committee of the whole, without any background information, for us to ask those questions which will produce the information we really want concerning the basic defence policy considerations which result in these estimates before us. That side of the problem has not been dealt with by the minister in the statement he just made. I do not think it could be dealt with except by adopting the procedure we have suggested before, and which the minister knows we have in mind; but I shall not press that matter now in view of the earlier decision.
There are some questions which were asked today and which, in the light of the minister's reply, I should like to follow up. I refer particularly to the question concerning the effect on our defence policy of the decisions taken at the London meeting of the Atlantic pact nations. This afternoon the minister said there would be no immediate consequences on our defence planning or defence program. As I recall his words this afternoon in that respect, he said that the formal adoption of the principle of balanced forces would not have an immediate effect on Canadian defence planning, because we have always regarded the defence of Canada as a part of the defence of an area, and the defence particularly of the North American continent. Then he went on to say, with respect to the question of commitments which Canada had accepted under the North Atlantic treaty, that we had undertaken no military commitments. I believe he doubted whether the working out of the Atlantic treaty would involve the acceptance by various powers of military commitments. If we are going to confine the word "commitment" to the dictionary meaning, I suppose that would be an acceptable answer. But surely, Mr. Chairman, if, as we are given to understand, the theory on which the Atlantic powers are working is that there shall be a joint over-all scheme of defence under which one of the powers when attacked will be immediately assisted and defended by the others, that calls for an over-all military planning. Surely it calls for the creation of planning and the preparation, in the initial stages on paper and later I would hope in being, of a joint or composite defence
Supply-National Defence force. If we are to have that defence force which will be available under any one of a given number of circumstances to defend any one of the Atlantic nations which may be attacked, then surely the joint over-all military command must know which nations are going to furnish which part of the forces, at least in a general way. Even though we may say we are not going to accept military commitments in the technical sense of the word, surely we are going to indicate we are prepared to accept certain responsibilities with respect to our contribution to that joint force. It is that aspect of the matter about which we are seeking information. What is the basis of Canada's approach? Which element or elements of the joint force does Canada feel she can best furnish? Which elements do the other nations with which we have been in consultation, and which elements do the Atlantic defence committee, feel Canada should undertake to furnish with respect to that joint effort?
In referring to my suggestion that there had been a change in emphasis resulting apparently from a change in policy with respect to the acquisition of equipment, the minister said that there had been no change in emphasis. He answered the comments I made this afternoon by saying the editorial in the Montreal Gazette to Which I had referred was based on an inaccurate interpretation of one of his earlier statements. Mr. Chairman, I did not criticize, nor did I intend to imply any criticism of, the emphasis being placed on equipment. What I did say was that statements made in recent months to the effect that a heavy proportion of our defence expenditure was going towards equipment did indicate to me, on the basis of a comparison with earlier statements, that there had been a change. We are now, as a matter of policy, concentrating heavy expenditures on equipment, whereas earlier we had said, and the minister referred to the statement he made two years ago which I think substantiates it, that in this changing world we should not commit ourselves to any formal design for our forces, or any substantial commitment on equipment, because we might find when we needed it in an emergency we were saddled with equipment of an obsolete type.

I can answer that question quickly, Mr. Chairman. There is no change yet in plan, because what is being done now was envisaged then. What I said at the time, after pointing to several dangers, was that there is a danger of getting large stocks of equipment that will become obsolete. But I did not say that we were not going to get any equipment. What has happened is that we have been using up stocks of equipment that we had left over from the war, and we have to replace them. In addition, aircraft and antisubmarine vessels that we were planning to construct in 1949, 1950, 1951, 1952 and 1953 were still in the design and development stage in 1947, 1948 and 1949. That is perfectly sensible, as the hon. member I am sure agrees.
I did not for a second suggest at that time that we should not require the equipment. But I would remind the house that in 1946 and 1947 it was not possible for us to spend all the appropriation that was voted by parliament at that time because of the rapid expansion of civilian industry and great need for civilian goods. At that time we felt that civilian needs took priority over military needs, particularly in view of the fact that we had considerable stocks left. But the next year that situation had eased and we moved into another period. We are now spending, as I say, 28 per cent on equipment. I should like to be spending more but I still think we are spending more proportionately than most of the other countries with which I am familiar.

But at the present time we feel that we are doing what we can.
With regard to this question of commitments, surely the hon. member and the committee recognize this fact. Staff planners may tote up a list of requirements in order to meet a possible act of attack or act of aggression in the year 1952 or 1953, showing a requirement for so many divisions, so many tanks, and so many aircraft. Then they look around to see where they can get them. That is a proper and necessary part of staff planning, and that is going on. speechtext: The minister intimated that he would welcome specific inquiries for information. I should like to make a specific inquiry about the department's policy with regard to Vernon camp. In view of the ideal situation of this camp and the great use to which it was put in the first and second wars, and in view of the fact that both the ground, the climate and the surroundings are ideal for proper training, especially as it is in the interior of British Columbia, and is not as vulnerable as it would be on the prairies or at the coast, I feel that the department has neglected this camp, which is its own asset. I should like to ask the minister if he contemplates, in the increased estimates, making greater use of that camp on a permanent basis and bringing people from the various parts of Canada to be trained there. There are available there facilities for long-range fire, for commando training, for hill climbing, for tank training and for practically every mode of defence training. Then the hon. member will have an opportunity for some little time.
This afternoon the Minister of National Defence stated that the information we had received in regard to the effect of the recent meeting in London was going to have no immediate effect on our preparation for national defence. Well, I think it would be well to refer back to what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said three days ago. Either his words were intended to convey some meaning, or they were not. I think hon. members gathered from those words, as the press of the country did, that there had been an important announcement which indicated a new concept of the relationship between the governments of the Atlantic area in dealing with this whole problem of the combined preservation of peace in the face of one threat, and one threat alone.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said on that occasion:
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, this is no less than the principle of the international division of labour to be applied amongst the members of the north Atlantic community for collective defence. We are now pledged-
Mark that word.
We are now pledged to do within the framework of the North Atlantic alliance what each of us has already been doing within our national defence system. We shall try to agree amongst ourselves which of us is the best able to concentrate on certain types of defence preparation.
This principle may come to mean the further application to defence, new techniques and tactics of scientific warfare: and eventually, possibly, to the abandonment of the old concept of defence by great masses of conscripted infantry, the bulk of which would be reservists called up on the outbreak of war.
That statement undoubtedly conveyed to the minds of many of us, as it very noticeably did to the editorial writers of a number of newspapers across the country, the idea that there was an intention here to allocate to each member nation a particular task that it could best perform in a combined military plan for the defence of our freedom. Then the minister went on to say:
In this planning allowance has to be made for the fact that certain states have commitments which are external to the north Atlantic area. Allowance has also to be made for the specially exposed position of some states to meet an initial attack.
And then the following words, it seems to me, presented to us a new idea of the role of different nations in relation to this pact.
3396	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence
These were his words:
The acceptance of "balanced collective forces" does not of course imply a strategy by which less exposed countries, or at least countries less exposed to ground attack, can collect their resources of men and material behind the ramparts of sacrifices made by others so that eventual victory can be achieved. North Atlantic strategy cannot mean, and our agreement does not imply, a strategy of liberation after destruction and occupation. There could be no hope for Europe in that strategy because the next time there may well be nothing to liberate.
Then he went on further to say:
The new principle recognizes, if I may pick out a purely hypothetical example, the waste and futility of one country trying to build battleships, let us say, if there are enough of these already in the navies of other members of the group. This principle in its turn must rest on the firm assurance that the other battleships, if I may continue that example, will be at your service if you need them.
Those words are not open to doubt. Either the minister of external affairs meant that or he was misinterpreting the situation. When he suggested that other battleships be used, obviously he intended that to apply to aircraft and to every defence arrangement. He then went on to say:
Therefore I think, Mr. Speaker, that this decision in favour of balanced collective forces is of vital importance. Of course it is a decision of principle only. Many bridges will have to be crossed before its application can be worked out in practice.
I think what hon. members had hoped we would hear today was an explanation of how we are going to cross those bridges and when and how this country is going to play its part in that broad concept of balanced forces. Obviously what the minister of external affairs was saying was that this agreement means that we are not again going to be in the position of waiting while sacrifice at some distant point makes it possible for the nations less ready to prepare themselves to defend their freedom. I am simply interpreting in clear terms exactly what the minister of external affairs said-a very important declaration. He pointed out something that should be apparent to everyone today. Unless the nations which join in this are ready to use whatever force is necessary and to use it immediately, there may be no second chance.
Between 1914 and 1918, which is within the memory of many members in this chamber, the German onslaught was held by the sacrifice of the armies of France, of Great Britain, of Italy and of the other allies who were not fully prepared to meet that test. Human flesh and blood paid the price of that unpreparedness in desperate numbers, but nevertheless they were able to hold on those long lines of trenches. The United States came into the war in 1917 and then the combined strength of the free nations overcame the German power.


In the last war the striking power of Germany was infinitely greater in its relative strength. When the time came they turned on France and the low countries. Opposed as they were by highly trained and well equipped British troops, they broke that line in a matter of days, and in weeks Belgium, Holland and France had capitulated. That happened within a time that not one of us ever dreamed a great nation would be called upon to accept defeat. The thing that saved this country and other countries was the incredible miscalculation Hitler made when he turned on Russia, and when Japan attacked the United States and the combined forces of the United States and Russia were brought side by side with those of the nations of the free world. But at that time it was touch and go.
Today science has advanced hitting power to a far greater degree than was known then. The only defence of freedom that is going to be effective is defence that can be put into operation immediately it is required. I fully accept the proposition put forward by the Minister of National Defence that at all times this parliament must be supreme. I do not think anyone challenges that or would challenge that. But the fact remains that the words of the minister of external affairs were intended to convey only one thought, that there was a clear expectation that these nations would stand together and that the decision of one nation not to build battleships when another nation was building them meant that that other nation relied on the nation with the battleships using them.
If a nation relied on another nation to build aircraft and abstained from building them because of that, that abstention would be based on the belief that the nation with the aircraft would use them in the common purpose. If a nation which because of special industrial skill or facilities was able to produce the largest quantities of armoured vehicles and heavy land machines of war and concentrated on that production while others did not, those nations that had not those instruments of war would rely on their being used. The words of the minister of external affairs could have no other interpretation or meaning. In fact, there could be no other meaning behind this agreement which is now regarded as one of the historical documents of modern history.

I must say that I am happy that I have won at least one convert and that I am receiving support at this stage from an hon. member who earlier was unconvinced. This country and the United States are separated from Europe by an ocean which offers us a great measure of protection, but that ocean which separates us from the continental areas also imposes real difficulties of transportation. That is one factor that must be recognized in the examination of this whole subject. In Europe west of the iron curtain there are over 200 million people, people who can provide and who obviously are ready to provide the armed masses which would stand against attack if it should come. What they would require in this allocation of tasks is that those nations which are some distance away should provide those powerful heavy forces which can move at great speed and in compact formation so that they can immediately support, if the dreadful necessity should ever arise, those land forces which are prepared to launch themselves against the land forces of the only enemy that could possibly threaten our freedom. Therefore it seems obvious that on this side of the Atlantic any development of this concept of balanced forces means that in this country we would concentrate on the air force and on fast hard-hitting armoured forces which could be quickly transported to Europe or to any other battlefield that might be found necessary as a result of events of this kind. There are always those who will suggest that when we actually contemplate the reality of these things we are talking in terms of war. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that in discussing it in this way we are talking in the only terms that will preserve peace. One thing that opens the possibility of war at any time is the belief in the minds of the aggressor that those who are strong enough to defend their freedom will nevertheless not stand together immediately to do that job as one combined defence team. The one thing that will preserve the peace for which so many men and women died a few years ago is the belief in the minds of those who direct the only aggressor force in the world today that all the forces of freedom will be immediately ranged against them if they should attempt the aggressive movement of their armed forces.
Unless we are prepared to talk in terms of what this means then we have no right to be dealing in dollars with figures of this kind. When in peacetime we are dealing in terms of $625 million in commitments we can only be dealing with that if we believe that war is a 55946-2154
Supply-National Defence danger, and that the only way we can hope to preserve peace is to make great expenditures of this kind. These expenditures are not for the purpose of having men and women in uniform. They are for the purpose of having men and women in uniform with equipment which will be effective in the event of their being required to use it. In this country today it is only necessary to ask how much of our armed force is in fact a hitting power in being and not simply a hitting power in preparation. Unless and until we have reached the point where whatever armed force we-maintain is ready to go into action immediately, then we are not actually carrying out our part of the joint agreement upon which the hope of peace now rests so greatly throughout the world, and that includes those on the other side of the iron curtain as well as ourselves.
In so far as the reserve army is concerned, the Minister of National Defence has spoken about the splendid spirit of those in the reserve forces, and that is something with which every single person will agree. In two world wars, and before that, Canadians have demonstrated that there are no finer fighting forces in the world when they have been trained and equipped to do the job which we hope will never be imposed upon Canadians again in our lifetime. Nevertheless when we look at the reserve army and the money that is to be spent on it we certainly should have a breakdown in these items, as between the active and reserve armies, a breakdown that is clear and understandable so that we can examine what is being done for the reserve army as well as for the active force. When it comes to the reserve army it is not enough simply to have figures of the enrolment in the reserve units. I for one want to know about the attendance at camp of the reserve units, and that is one of the details I propose to ask for. I want to know what the average attendance of the enrolment of the reserve units is, because without that we do not know what the figures mean. The mere entering of a name on the enrolment books does not tell us the story.
At the present time our infantry units, with their great traditions behind them, are carrying out exercises with as high a degree of realism as is possible under the limitations that they must face. Very frequently they carry out their exercises over week ends. They do their drills in the various armouries across the country, and they get their firing practice and other training in camps in varying degrees depending upon where they are. So it is with: the other units, but do not let anybody be: under the impression that they are gettingtraining which has brought them anywhere near the point that they could be put into the

This is the sixth summer after V-E day, and yet in the sixth summer after victory in Europe no firing practice will be carried out at the artillery camps across the country because they have not yet reached the stage where that has become a practical possibility.

I will not enter into a debate about it. I will give the minister the information because I made inquiries about it only today. There is no need for us to exchange views on the matter because we can both satisfy ourselves in regard to the point. In so far as this training is concerned, it is not training that has reached the point where there would not be a very long time required to prepare these men for the field. The minister has said that the objective of the training is to bring them in conformity with the active forces as soon as possible, and that is a high objective. We have as fine men and women in uniform as anywhere in the world. On the grounds in front of the parliament buildings a few days ago most of those in this chamber saw the presentation of the colours to the Royal Canadian Air Force. They saw men in drill formation going through movements comparable with any they would see in the guards parade in London, or anywhere else in the world. Nevertheless, no matter how high a degree of skill may be shown in drill or anything of that kind, it does not meet the requirements unless we have those forces actually ready to take their part. I think it is essential that we know what percentage of the forces is immediately ready for active service if they should be called upon, and how many are in various stages of training, so that we who are called upon to vote the money may know what it is we are voting it for. After all, under our system of parliamentary government there is no single thing which so much tests the real functioning of our parliament as the exercise of full


control of expenditures. There is no single function of parliament over which parliament has so jealously exercised that control as over the expenditures for the armed forces. It will be recalled that it was the allocation of money for armed forces that began our present period of parliamentary responsibility several hundred years ago. Parliament is in duty bound to find out what the facts are, and in duty bound not to accept broad assurances, no matter what their regard may be for any minister or for those associated with him.
This country has great opportunities to economize, while at the same time greatly increasing its military strength. In this country there is an opportunity for training air forces, and training fast hard-hitting land forces as well. So far as armoured units are concerned, we have the space in which they can train; in which they can move over great distances and gain a sense of manoeuvrability which was such a decisive factor in the last war. It was no accident of circumstance that General Patton made that tremendous sweep up from Brittany, which had such an effect on the whole course of the war in Europe. His armoured forces had been training in the great spaces of the southern United States. They were accustomed to sweeping movement at a speed that had never been contemplated by those trained in restricted areas. In this country men could be trained in armoured vehicles to move hundreds or thousands of miles if necessary, with hard-hitting power and at the highest of speeds. It also affords a place to train air force personnel, not only our own but those who would be associated with us, and not only in combat formation, bombing and navigation, as well as in the naval defence service, but in all the combined operations which form part of the great air movements today. This continent is the place where fast-moving and hard-hitting forces, whether in the air or on the land, could be trained, in a way that they could be trained in no other country in the world. In case anyone says, why could they not be trained in Africa or South America or Australia, the answer is that on this continent we have these great training areas in close proximity to the great producing plants where the largest number of motor vehicles in the world are turned out each year. Consequently these opportunities present themselves not only for training our own forces, but for training fast-hitting forces in the air and on the land of the combined nations which met in London a short time ago.
I do hope that in dealing with this the Minister of National Defence will not take

with any spirit of resentment the suggestion that there could be improvement. We do not want to see a repetition of what we saw on two other occasions, when attempts to bring up questions about items in the estimates were immediately presented as votes of confidence, and consequently placed in the position where there could be no free consideration of those votes. Let us examine this with full recognition of the vital importance of the subject we are discussing. I do earnestly hope that the minister will indicate there is some intention of examining our present structure so that there can be a reallocation of forces in keeping with the statement of the minister of external affairs only three days ago. There is no reason at all to believe that substantial economies might not be effected if we really followed a plan of concentrating on those things for which we could best train the armed forces.
In so far as the estimates themselves are concerned, I shall close these remarks by indicating a way in which I think the Minister of National Defence could save a great deal of time. He pointed out that in Westminster they set aside four days for the consideration of the defence estimates. We have only had a part of two days, so even if we move as expeditiously as they do in Westminster we still have more than two days left to consider these estimates. What we must remember is that the British house considers the defence estimates in four days because those defence estimates have already been before a subcommittee on estimates, before which the senior staff officers have appeared and been examined on the expenditures. This subject, therefore, has been reviewed just in the way other matters have been reviewed. Yesterday the Minister of National Defence expressed great satisfaction with the result of a committee which met to examine the defence bills that were before the house. The committee had the staff officers before it, and made some amendments in the bill. As a result of this combined effort, legislation emerged which quickly passed through this house. The government has seen fit, however, to oppose the appointment of such a committee. Nevertheless, there are still ways in which time could be saved.
I would suggest that time could be saved if the minister would give instructions to have a statement prepared showing the number of units, active and reserve, of the army, navy and air force, divided into the different types of unit in each of those branches. In the case of the army, that would call for a statement of the number of infantry units; the number of artillery units; the number of
Supply-National Defence armoured units; the number of reconnaissance units, and the number of engineering units, in one column. Then there would be a statement of equipment which they should have, and in another column what they have; or if he will give it in terms of percentage even, that will be very helpful. In the case of the air force he should give the number of squadrons, fighter squadrons and bomber squadrons-no, we could leave that out. He could show the several types and the number of machines, and the personnel in each case. In the case of the navy, the ships and the personnel on those ships. Then, in relation to those divisions the expenditures to be devoted to each branch of the service during the present year, there should also be a statement showing the headquarters across this country, the personnel at each of the headquarters, and the amount that is being asked for the maintenance of those headquarters, the same as for the headquarters at Ottawa. Mr. Chairman, that would be in keeping with the type of information that is made available by other departments, and an examination of that would enable us to discuss these estimates with some knowledge of what is actually before us.
Then, in the case of buildings, there should be a statement prepared in exactly the same manner as that prepared by the Department of Public Works, showing the naval barracks at Charlottetown, if that is to be built this year; showing buildings of any kind that are to be erected in any part of this country. After all, these buildings are just as important as post offices and other buildings of that kind which are included in the details of the estimates by other departments.
Now, this information can be given. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is the kind of information we should have. It is certainly not more than we should have. From that we could then proceed to ask what the state of the training is of these various units, with knowledge of the type of units we are discussing; of the number of personnel involved; and why that money is required. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I conclude these remarks with the earnest suggestion that the minister state that he will do this, and that before we again consider these estimates that information will be before us.

In the manoeuvres held late last fall, all maps and charts were duplicates of similar territory in Canada. The exercises were based upon the theory that simultaneous attacks were being conducted against twelve Canadian centres.
If this statement is true, and this article gives the name of the individual and everything, it would appear as though we were not too far away from the necessity of having all our airports in condition to handle the heavy bombers of today.
The minister might also think of the Torbay airport which was used so extensively in the last war by the R.C.A.F. The runways there, generally speaking, are unable to accommodate safely the large bombers. The other item is in connection with the reserve units now being formed in Newfoundland. From the return I was given, as it is set out at page 1569 of Hansard, the total strength of the regular army in Newfoundland is 52, consisting of 9 officers and 43 men. There are two reserve regiments now being formed. I am told in connection with the training of these reserves that there are no instructors available, and that the only personnel there capable of giving instruction are headquarters staff. I do not know whether that is so now, but that was the position in the middle of March when I was given the information. If that condition has not changed I do submit that some personnel qualified for that purpose should be sent there.
I do not believe at present they have enough men to do the training. I do not know what happened in connection with the naval installation. Last session when I mentioned this to the minister I believe he told me they were taking over some 22 naval installations and contemplated putting some in service. The minister can reassure us as to the situation. I believe he said at that time that the installation at Bay Bulls was going to be left in private hands.
The other point is that at the airport at Gander, and I presume also at Torbay, there is nothing in the way of protection. I am dealing with this matter perhaps in an amateurish way, because I do not know very much about it. However, it appears to me it might be wise to have at least a small mobile force there used to the terrain and the whole countryside. I do not know whether that is practical or not. I understand that it would not be practical to have

large forces in all places where there might be attack, but I should think it would not be too difficult or too expensive at a vulnerable airport to have a highly trained mobile force. I pass that along for what it is worth.
