speechtext:
Replying to the hon. member for St. John's East, as he knows, the question of Gander airport comes within the Department of Transport, because it operates that airfield. My recollection of the runways, from having been there, is that they are considered quite adequate for any present-day use, and that they are in good condition.	-
We have no present intention of enlarging or extending the runways at Torbay. The main Royal Canadian Air Force installation in that part of the world is at Goose Bay, where we have one of the greatest airports, built entirely by Canada, and with long and first class runways. There, in addition to the Canadian air force, there is a considerable strength of the United States air force.
On the island itself there are three United States bases, one at Fort Pepperell, one at Argentia, which is a joint air and naval base, and one at Harmon field, which is an air base. I feel that in the interest of a balanced collective force we should not add to the number of existing major airfields in Newfoundland at the present time. They are adequate for all the needs we can see ahead.
With regard to the defence of the field at Gander, the observations of the hon. member made on the same point in November were taken into consideration, and I discussed this question again with my advisers. Generally speaking it is not considered that the installation of a unit even as small as a company would be justified for that purpose at that place.
With regard to the other defence forces, the 52 in the regular army consist of staff, administrative and training officers and also supply services. It is not planned to increase those numbers in any considerable degree. The staff is considered to be quite adequate for the job. They will provide administrative and training staffs for the units, and I believe they will be found to be quite adequate.
In connection with the organization of units, as will be remembered, we established H.M.C.S. Cabot as a unit of the naval reserve. It had a strength on April 26 of 70 officers and men, including a very considerable number of officers in the neighbourhood of St. John's who served with the Canadian navy during the war. We also have 20 cadets at Memorial university who have entered the University Naval Training Division, and there have been established three units of the reserve army, 55946-216
Supply-National Defence consisting of the Royal Newfoundland Regiment, the 166th Field Regiment of the R.C.A. and the 56th Independent Field Squadron of the R.C.E. These were organized in January 1950. We have already very encouraging enrolments of officers, non-commissioned officers and men. This indicates that what the hon. member has said about the good spirit in Newfoundland is quite true. We are getting recruits there in considerable numbers and of good quality, and we hope before the end of this year to have these three army units and the navy unit organized on a sound footing. This is the first time that there will be any reserve navy or army units in existence in Newfoundland. I understand that neither prior to the first war nor in between the first and second wars were there any reserve units there. This represents a very considerable advance.
This work of organization has been greatly facilitated by the encouragement of former officers. I met them myself in St. John's on July 1 last, and I also met representatives of the municipalities and industries and Legion branches at Corner Brook and Grand Falls, where we are putting up armouries. When they are completed, as I expect they will be at an early date, we expect that there will be sub-units of these units established there, in a healthy condition.
We have established a permanent headquarters at Buckmaster's field with adequate buildings for all services. We have a cadet corps, a C.O.T.C. unit in connection with the university, and we have also recruited officers and men for the active force. Altogether Newfoundland has responded very well indeed to the appeals made.

speechtext: I wish to make only a few remarks. We have listened to the debate today with much interest and have heard practically every subject discussed, from the chaplain service to the general defence of Canada. So far as chaplain service is concerned, I agree entirely with what the minister said, that the chaplains should have officer rank. I .have had some experience with chaplains in my army experience, and I am sure that the minister's idea is absolutely correct. There is no reason why the chaplain service should not be treated the same as the medical or the dental service. I used to think that it would be a good idea if chaplains had a little more military training because possibly the sloppiest salutes you saw in the army were those given by some chaplains.

They usually did that. A good chaplain looked after his men and provided sports and so on, which is another reason why he should have a higher rank than that of an N.C.O.
I do not think the minister should feel too badly over the criticism there has been of his estimates. I think he must admit that both inside and outside the house there is support for his estimates. But we would like to know what the money is being spent for. I do not think anyone is suggesting that the estimates should be reduced. I can remember before the last war when the estimates amounted to only $30 million or $40 million, but there would be long debates and many hon. members seemed anxious to have the estimates not passed. There were members who belonged to the government side, the same government that is in power now, who asked to have the estimates reduced to $1. I think the Minister of National Defence has practically 100 per cent support. He can hardly complain if there is an interest shown in his estimates and if members want to know just why the estimates are to be passed.
In 1939, before the last war there was considerable isolationism in this country which is not to be found today. As far as defence is concerned I think the people from one end of Canada to the other feel that there is a necessity for the defence of this country. Both before the first great war and the second great war we perhaps felt we could rely on Great Britain and the British navy, but that is not the case today. A great deal has been said about the possibility of Canada being attacked should war start. I was interested in reading an article not so long ago which was dated in January of this year. The article stated that considerable attention is being given in the European press to the observation of Brigadier X, that in a future war the first soviet blow would be dealt against Canada. The article refers to another article in a Netherlands daily which stated that Canada would be the objective of a soviet invasion. It was stated that the military experts of the United States and Canada have good reason to realize the danger of a soviet invasion of the North American continent and that recently the Canadian people were faced with this hard reality by an article in The Ensign by Brigadier X.
We in Canada along with the United States are responsible for the defence of the
North American continent. That is probably the chief obligation of Canada. I was sorry I was not in the chamber this afternoon when Exercise Sweetbriar was being discussed. We must ask ourselves what is the situation as far as the defence of the northern part of this continent is concerned. We are only a short distance from Asia and we are told that in Siberia there are 25 million Russians. That country has the same area as Alaska, which along with the northern part of Canada supports a population of only one million. We are told also that Russia retains about twenty divisions in the northern Siberia country. This gives us some idea of just what danger there is should Russia decide to attack from that quarter.
It also impresses upon Canada the necessity of training for defence in the north country. We know that this was realized by the Department of National Defence and the defence council because they have trained men in northern Canada along with the United States forces. Some 5,000 spent a few weeks in northern Canada last year and they came through their short training quite well. I understand that many things were learned by the defence departments of Canada and the United States and the minister might well tell us some of the lessons that were learned with regard to defence in the north.
We hear that the Russians are training the natives of the Aleutian islands and the Eskimos in Russia for scout duties and to act as glacier outpost patrols. When the minister speaks later I should like him to state whether Canada, and possibly the United States along with Canada, is making any attempt to train the Eskimo or those who live in the northern sections of Canada and Alaska.
